+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan had spent twenty years listening to machines announce their approaching failures. This one sounded healthy, which removed the only explanation he would have welcomed for the armed men aboard. “What happens,” he asked, “if I decline the invitation?” The officer opposite him adjusted a spotless cuff. “We return you home.” “Before or after the meeting?” “After, naturally.” Arthur looked through the observation port. Mars had become a rusty coin beneath them. Somewhere on it, his breakfast remained under a warming hood, consuming electricity he could no longer afford. “You broke my front-door seal.” “The Corps will reimburse you.” “Your men said that about the greenhouse.” “The greenhouse obstructed our landing.” “It generally obstructs things trying to land in it.” The officer smiled without embarrassment. On his collar, the silver scorpion of the Antares Diplomatic Corps clasped a seven-pointed star. Arthur remembered six points from the recruiting posters. “New insignia?” “New jurisdiction.” “That sounds expensive.” “It has been.” *** Their destination was a cylindrical station unmarked on the passenger chart. Its central spindle shone against the stars; habitation drums revolved around it with the ponderous assurance of machinery built when steel had been cheaper than freight. In the docking gallery, an electric clock displayed GREENWICH STANDARD. Beneath it, someone had pasted a notice: PLEASE CONSERVE PAPER CUPS. Arthur found this reassuring until he noticed the gun emplacements. The officer conducted him through two pressure doors into an office furnished with green leather chairs. A woman sat behind a steel desk, studying a strip of perforated tape. “Mr. Neegan. I am Commissioner Senn.” “Commissioner of what?” “For this afternoon, disputed property.” “Mine?” “That is the question.” She indicated a chair. The officer remained beside the door. “I’d prefer him outside,” Arthur said. “So would I,” said Senn. “Unfortunately, he represents our allies.” “Antares?” “A portion of it.” The officer’s expression did not change. Arthur sat. Senn pressed a switch. A globe of Mars glimmered above the desk, its inhabited districts outlined in blue. His own holding appeared as a yellow square, ludicrously large at that scale. “That isn’t accurate.” “It is politically accurate. Geographical accuracy would make it invisible.” “What do you want?” “To offer you forty million terrestrial credits.” Arthur rested both hands on his knees. “For the plot?” “For granting extraction rights to a trust whose beneficiaries will be the indentured workers of Mars.” He looked at the officer. “Since when does Antares concern itself with miners?” “Since this morning,” said Senn. “Circumstances have improved our principles.” *** A steward brought coffee in porcelain cups. Arthur turned his over. “No paper shortage here?” “The notice applies to junior personnel.” “So will the principles, I imagine.” Senn waited until the steward had gone. “Your assay reached the Colonial Bureau on Tuesday. On Wednesday, eleven corporations filed claims against your title. By Thursday, three governments had discovered strategic obligations toward Mars.” “My title predates the corporations.” “Yes. They find that particularly objectionable.” “And your trust makes everything respectable?” “No. It makes annexation inconvenient. Confiscating one settler’s land is an administrative matter. Confiscating the collective property of two hundred thousand labourers invites disturbances in the mines.” “Indentured labourers aren’t permitted to own mineral rights.” “Individually.” Arthur studied her. “That omission has been there for sixty years,” she said. “Nobody expected them to buy any.” “And forty million buys my cooperation.” “Forty million buys your rights. Your cooperation requires an explanation.” She touched another switch. The globe vanished. A jagged line crossed the air above the desk. “Your Azra sample was tested beside a standard radioactive source. Decay accelerated, as expected. Then it stopped accelerating.” “The sample was exhausted?” “Azra is not consumed.” “The source, then.” “No.” Arthur leaned forward. Senn continued. “At precisely the same instant, an assay specimen on Luna altered its behaviour. So did a specimen aboard an Antarean cruiser.” “Instrument interference.” “That was our first explanation.” “And your second?” “We are still discussing whether we dare have one.” *** The filtration hummed behind the walls. Arthur said, “You think the deposits communicate.” “We know they respond together. Communication implies a purpose.” “Who else knows?” “Enough people to make you valuable. Not enough to make you safe.” The officer spoke for the first time. “Commissioner, the military findings remain restricted.” “Then you should not have brought a mining engineer.” Arthur ignored him. “My deposit isn’t a vein.” Senn’s fingers tightened around her cup. “Explain.” “The bore readings repeat. Rich material, barren interval, rich material. I assumed folding, but the intervals are too regular. I requested deeper soundings.” “Cancel them.” “They’re automatic.” “When?” Arthur glanced at the Greenwich clock, converted reluctantly, and felt his mouth grow dry. “Four hours.” Senn reached for the desk telephone. The officer put a hand on it. “Our agreement requires consultation before interference with survey operations.” For a moment neither moved. Arthur said, “Your allies want it drilled.” “Some of them,” Senn replied. “And you want a labour trust standing between them and the drill.” “I want a legal owner able to demand a suspension without declaring war.” Arthur rose. “Put the telephone down.” The officer looked mildly surprised. “You have no authority here.” “No. But apparently I have some on Mars.” *** Senn slid a document across the desk. Its pages were thin, closely typed, and already bore several signatures. Arthur read the first paragraph, then the last. “Add a condition.” “Which?” “No extraction without approval by the beneficiaries.” “That could prevent production indefinitely.” “Yes.” The officer said, “The fleet will not protect an idle mine.” Arthur looked at his seven-pointed badge. “Then you’ll have to explain to the other portions of Antares why.” Senn’s smile was brief and entirely genuine. She drew the telephone toward her. While she dictated, Arthur listened to the station’s machinery. Somewhere beneath its decks, almost certainly, an Azra-assisted pile supplied their light and air. He wished he had asked what time the lunar specimen had changed.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Asimov's style and successfully creates a tense political thriller set in a well-realized sci-fi universe. The author captures Asimov's trademark blend of intimate human drama with vast cosmic implications, particularly in the revelation that Azra deposits across the solar system respond simultaneously - a classic "big picture" concept emerging from seemingly small observations. The dialogue is exceptionally well-crafted, carrying most of the narrative weight while revealing character, advancing plot, and building tension. Each character has a distinct voice: Arthur's practical engineering mindset, Senn's calculated political maneuvering, and the officer's military formality. The conversations feel natural while efficiently conveying complex political and scientific information. The world-building is subtle but effective, using small details like the modified insignia, paper cup conservation notices, and Greenwich Standard time to suggest a lived-in universe with its own bureaucratic absurdities. The retrofuturistic elements (perforated tape, steel desks, porcelain cups) successfully evoke classic sci-fi aesthetics. The pacing is excellent, building from Arthur's initial confusion through the revelation of the forty million credit offer to the disturbing implications of synchronized Azra behavior. The chapter ends on a perfect note of uncertainty and foreboding without false resolution. However, the piece occasionally relies on exposition delivered through dialogue, though this is handled more skillfully than in most attempts. Some descriptions, while atmospheric, border on being overly sparse in places where more vivid imagery might enhance the scene. The political intrigue feels authentic and complex, with multiple factions having believable motivations. Arthur's character development from confused victim to someone asserting agency feels earned and natural. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 88.0
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Darkroom Revelations Under the safelight, Elliot’s silver rings looked like wounds in the red. That was the kind of sentence I would have written in my process journal, then crossed out for trying too hard. In person, I said, “Your hand’s in the developer.” “Only the glove.” “Still. We’ve discussed becoming one with the medium.” He smiled without looking up. His eyeliner had survived eleven hours better than my patience usually survived eleven minutes. I’d been watching him all semester. Not creepily, I hoped. Academically, at first: his photographs made empty bus shelters seem embarrassed to be empty. Then less academically. The thrifted mesh sleeves under enormous band shirts. The trousers repaired with violet thread. His habit of listening until people accidentally said what they meant. At twenty-five, I generally knew when I wanted somebody. I wore orange boots, shaved one side of my head, and asked people out before they finished wondering whether I might. With Elliot, nineteen and quiet enough to make silence feel deliberate, I kept finding reasons to discuss aperture. Tonight our final project occupied every dry surface: double portraits, one chosen by the subject, one chosen by the photographer. “Your turn,” I said, lifting a test print with the tongs. “Tell me what’s wrong with this one.” He leaned closer. His shoulder brushed mine. “Nothing technically.” “An execution-worthy compliment.” “It looks like you already decided who I am.” I put the print down. In it, he stood beneath the railway bridge, chin raised, coat hanging from his narrow shoulders. I’d loved the severe geometry. The almost confrontational beauty. “What did I decide?” “That I’m confident.” “You look confident.” “Yeah.” The extractor fan rattled above us. Somewhere outside, a cart squeaked down the corridor. I wanted to rescue the conversation. Usually that meant making a joke, issuing a new instruction, getting us moving again. Instead, I said, “Do you want another version?” He worried a loose stitch at his cuff. “I don’t know what version I want.” “Of the picture?” A small, uneasy laugh. “Of me, maybe.” I stayed against the counter. Giving him room felt strangely like doing nothing, and doing nothing had never been my talent. “Okay,” I said. “I’ve been thinking about gender.” The word seemed louder than the fan. “Not because of the clothes,” he added quickly. “Or not only. I know boys can wear whatever. I’ve given myself that lecture.” “I wasn’t going to.” “I know. Sorry.” “You don’t have to apologize.” He glanced at me. “You say that like an order.” I winced. He smiled. “Occupational hazard,” I said. “Being insufferable.” For a moment, we could breathe again. He told me about trying different names in an old notebook, then feeling ridiculous and tearing out the page. About sometimes liking being called a boy, sometimes feeling as though someone had handed him a coat that almost fit. About not knowing whether he wanted to change anything publicly. “I’m still fine with he,” he said. “For now.” “Okay.” “You can say more than okay.” “I’m trying not to give you a five-point plan.” “Oh. Thank you.” His gratitude stung. I hadn’t done anything except resist taking over. And beneath my concern, inconveniently alive, was excitement. I wanted to see the photographs he might make when he stopped correcting himself before pressing the shutter. I wanted to know which name had survived longest in the notebook. I also wanted to kiss him. That was where everything tangled. My attractions usually announced themselves clearly: women with deliberate swagger, men whose softness sat comfortably inside being men. People who seemed to know what they were offering, and let me decide whether to reach. Elliot hadn’t offered certainty. He hadn’t even offered romance. Yet there I was, wondering what wanting him said about me, as though his confession required an immediate revision of my biography. “I should tell you something,” I said. He straightened. “I’ve been trying to impress you for approximately nine weeks.” His mouth opened. Then he laughed. “The lecture about archival washing?” “That was unfortunately sincere.” “And the orange boots?” “Those predate you.” He looked down, smiling now in a way I hadn’t photographed. “I thought you just liked telling me what to do.” “I do. I’m working on expanding my repertoire.” He reached behind him for a towel and knocked his elbow against the light switch. White light flooded the room. “Shit,” we said together. I slapped the switch off. Too late. On the counter, beside the open black bag, lay our remaining stack of photographic paper. For several seconds, neither of us moved. Then Elliot whispered, “Could we pretend that didn’t happen?” I lifted the top sheet. Blank, expensive, ruined. “Conceptually?” He covered his face. I started laughing. Not gracefully. The exhausted, helpless kind that bent me over the counter. After a horrified second, he joined me. “We had six sheets left,” he said. “We had six sheets.” “I’ll replace them.” “We’ll replace them. Tomorrow.” The loss punctured something useful. There was no perfect session left to preserve. Elliot lowered his hands. “For the other portrait, could I choose your clothes?” “Yes.” “Not tonight.” “Tomorrow,” I said. He stepped closer, then stopped. I waited, resisting the urge to turn his hesitation into a decision. “Are you still trying to impress me?” “Less successfully now.” “Dani.” My name sounded different when he wasn’t asking about an assignment. “Can I kiss you?” “Yes.” His rings caught my sleeve. The kiss was brief and slightly misplaced; we both turned the same way, corrected, laughed against each other. Afterward, I didn’t ask what it meant. He picked up my rejected portrait and studied it. “I don’t hate this,” he said. “I just want more than one.” “I’d like to make more.” “With me directing.” I handed him the print. “Your turn.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and emotional intelligence in handling a delicate subject matter. The narrative successfully captures Dani's voice as an assertive art student while showing her vulnerability when confronted with unfamiliar territory. The darkroom setting is expertly utilized both literally and metaphorically, creating an intimate confessional space that feels authentic to the photography context. The characterization is particularly strong. Dani's internal conflict between her natural take-charge personality and her desire to give Elliot agency feels genuine and well-developed. Her self-awareness about her tendency to be controlling ("You say that like an order") adds depth and prevents her from becoming a one-dimensional character. Elliot's vulnerability and tentative self-exploration is handled with sensitivity, avoiding both melodrama and oversimplification. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, with realistic awkwardness and humor that lightens heavy moments without undermining their significance. The conversation about gender identity unfolds organically rather than feeling like an information dump. The banter between the characters establishes their chemistry effectively. The prose style is clean and evocative without being overwrought. Lines like "Under the safelight, Elliot's silver rings looked like wounds in the red" establish atmosphere without excessive purple prose. The writing maintains consistent quality throughout, with strong imagery rooted in the photography setting. The pacing builds tension effectively, using the darkroom work as a natural framework for intimate conversation. The accidental exposure of the photographic paper serves as both a plot device and metaphor, creating a moment of shared vulnerability that allows the relationship to progress naturally. The ending feels earned rather than forced. The kiss emerges from genuine connection and mutual interest, and the final exchange about making more portraits provides satisfying closure while suggesting future development. The transformation in their relationship feels gradual and believable. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly self-conscious, and a few instances where the metaphorical weight of the photography setting feels slightly heavy-handed. However, these are minor issues in an otherwise accomplished piece. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 78.4
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
At nine seventeen, Ben stepped backward off a Roman pavement to improve his view of a church and nearly became a footnote. Brakes shrieked. A motorcycle stopped beside his knee. “Ma sei scemo? The pavement! That raised thing! What do you imagine it’s for?” Ben clutched his guidebook. “Mi dispiace. Sono molto… embarrassed.” “Obviously.” The rider pushed up her visor. Dark eyes, crooked mouth, a small white scar through one eyebrow. Her motorcycle had a turquoise tank with a spectacular yellow scrape down one side. “Are you hurt?” he asked. She looked at him, then at the motorcycle. “Emotionally. She hates tourists.” “I’m an academic.” “Worse. Tourists eventually go home.” Behind them, somewhere beyond the narrow streets, the Trevi Fountain roared. Ben’s guidebook fell open in the gutter. She picked it up before he could. “‘Discover the authentic Rome,’” she read. “You were discovering the underside of a bus.” He laughed, unexpectedly loudly. Her mouth changed. *** At nine forty, Alessandra ordered his coffee because his attempt had accidentally requested a grandfather. “Nonno, not lungo,” she explained. “You want a long coffee, not an elderly relative.” “I teach medieval history.” “And yet.” They stood at the bar. She drank her espresso in one movement; he waited for his to cool. Her phone kept vibrating against the marble. “Work?” he asked. “People paying me to take things where they could have taken them themselves.” “A public service.” “A tragic failure of public transport.” She silenced the phone. When the bartender turned away, her fingers closed around a tiny silver-coloured spoon. It vanished into her jacket with the absent ease of someone tucking back her hair. Ben glanced at her pocket. “What?” she said. “Nothing.” “That will get you into trouble here.” Outside, she handed him a spare helmet. “I have a perfectly adequate itinerary,” he said. She opened his guidebook. “Three churches before lunch? What have you done that needs forgiving?” *** By ten fifteen, he had learned that “hold on” was not a metaphor. “Not the jacket,” she shouted. “Me.” He placed his hands carefully at her waist. “I’m not a museum exhibit. You can touch.” Rome broke into hot fragments: laundry, brake lights, an orange smashed beneath a van. At a red light, a woman in a tiny car disputed Alessandra’s existence with both hands. Alessandra blew her a kiss. “Friend of yours?” Ben asked. “We’re becoming close.” He noticed the yellow damage again when they stopped. “What happened to the tank?” “A misunderstanding.” “With something yellow?” “You historians need everything explained.” Her dispatcher called. She answered, listened, and said, “After lunch,” three times with increasing optimism. Then she switched off the phone. “Are you allowed to do that?” “No.” *** At eleven, she delivered an envelope to a severe building near the river and emerged carrying two visitor badges. “Why two?” “Souvenirs.” “Alessandra.” She looked delighted. “Already the disappointed voice.” She took him upstairs before anyone could disagree. On a quiet landing, an unlatched door opened onto a terrace crowded with air-conditioning units. Beyond them lay domes, aerials, roof gardens; Rome untidy and enormous. “This isn’t public,” Ben whispered. “Then speak privately.” He edged away from the parapet. “Afraid of heights?” “Mostly of falling.” She climbed onto a low concrete plinth, arms spread. “Come on, Professor.” “No.” “Such a small word.” “A useful one.” For a moment she studied him without smiling. Then she stepped down. “All right.” It was the first thing she had done that made him want to kiss her. *** At one, they ate pizza folded in greasy paper beside the Tiber. “What does sabbatical mean?” she asked. “Technically, time for research.” “And untechnically?” He watched a plastic bottle turn in an eddy. “Time to discover whether I still like the thing I’ve spent twenty years doing.” She stopped chewing. “How old are you?” “Thirty-eight.” “Twenty years?” “I was an unusually boring adolescent.” “I was trouble.” “Past tense?” She stole a mushroom from his pizza. “My mother cleans holiday apartments,” she said. “She’s started leaving Rome on Sundays because she says she can’t bear people enjoying it.” “Do you?” “Sometimes.” He waited. She crumpled her paper. “Sometimes I like showing off.” *** At three, rain trapped them beneath a bookstall’s awning. Alessandra tried on a pair of red sunglasses displayed beside the postcards. “Too much?” she asked. “For what?” “Exactly.” The bookseller was arguing with someone under the next canopy. Alessandra pushed the glasses into her hair and began walking. Ben stayed where he was. She turned. Rain silvered her lashes. “What now?” He looked at the glasses. Something shut behind her face. “Oh, relax. I’m bringing them back.” “Then bring them back.” Traffic hissed past. For the first time all day, she seemed unsure what to do with her hands. She returned the glasses to their stand. “You’re very English.” “Not exclusively.” Outside the awning, she walked beside him rather than ahead. *** At six, on the Janiculum, he rang his university colleague. “Yes, the archive was useful,” he said, watching Alessandra attempt to balance a pinecone on her nose. “No, I haven’t finished the proposal.” A pause. “No. I can’t do it tonight.” He ended the call. Alessandra caught the falling pinecone. “Was that rebellion?” “Administrative rebellion.” “Still counts.” *** At ten, she brought him back to his hotel. Neither removed their helmet. “Thank you,” he said. “You say that too much.” “I’ve had practice.” She reached beneath his chin and undid the strap. Her fingers lingered there; his careful farewell deserted him. “May I—” “Yes, Ben.” The kiss was brief, warm, faintly awkward around the helmets. Afterward she took the café spoon from her pocket and pressed it into his palm. “Tomorrow,” she said. “We should return that.” Then she rode away before he could ask whether she meant it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates two distinct characters - Alessandra, the fiery Roman motorcycle courier with kleptomaniac tendencies, and Ben, the polite British academic - and develops their relationship through a series of interconnected scenes spanning a single day in Rome. The structure works well, using time stamps to create discrete vignettes that build momentum. The dialogue is particularly strong, capturing the cultural and personality differences between the characters through natural-sounding exchanges. Alessandra's sharp wit ("Tourists eventually go home." "Worse. Tourists eventually go home.") contrasts effectively with Ben's more formal, apologetic manner. The author handles the kleptomania subplot with appropriate subtlety - the stolen spoon at the café, the sunglasses incident, and the final gesture of giving Ben the spoon create a thread that reveals character without being heavy-handed. The tension around the sunglasses scene is particularly well-executed, showing Ben's moral boundaries and Alessandra's reaction to being judged. The prose style is clean and economical, avoiding purple prose while still creating vivid imagery ("Rome broke into hot fragments: laundry, brake lights, an orange smashed beneath a van"). The pacing moves well between action, dialogue, and quieter character moments. However, the piece has some limitations. While competently executed, it follows fairly predictable romantic comedy beats - the meet-cute, the tour of the city, moments of tension and reconciliation, the parting kiss. The character development, while solid, doesn't venture into particularly surprising territory. Ben's transformation from cautious academic to someone willing to break rules feels somewhat expected, though it's handled believably. The emotional complexity is present but not deeply explored. Alessandra's motivations remain appropriately enigmatic, but we don't get much sense of deeper vulnerability or complexity beyond her mischievous exterior. Ben's sabbatical crisis is mentioned but not fully developed as an emotional thread. The ending works within the genre conventions but doesn't offer particular surprise or insight. The gesture with the spoon is sweet but feels like a standard romantic setup for future encounters. Overall, this is solid, professional-level writing that fulfills its brief competently without reaching exceptional heights of creativity or emotional depth. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.8
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the time the stranger sits down, I have prevented one duel, encouraged one proposal, and watered the basil with something that probably isn’t whisky. The basil is humming. I choose not to investigate. “Vega whisky, neat,” the stranger says. “Better make that a double.” His tentacled dreads are tangled around the collar of his travel coat. One clutches a baggage ticket. Another appears to be comforting a third. “Bad crossing?” I ask. “Bad destination.” “That costs extra.” He looks up. “The joke, not the whisky.” “Oh.” He considers this. “Put both on my tab.” Behind him, The Last Outpost carries on being home. Miners settle into heated benches. Merchants cheat at cards beneath our artificial lemon tree. Beyond the windows, the asteroid belt turns slowly through the outermost dark of Andromeda. I pour generously. Generosity is one of my talents. Accurate inventory is one of my flaws. “Nets,” calls Brindle from table six, “tell Ollo you can’t propose marriage with a replacement air filter.” “Was it the right filter?” “Obviously,” Ollo says. “Then I’d hear him out.” The stranger watches them. “Do you own this place?” “No. I just know which pipes need threats.” “I need the owner.” “That’ll be Mara. She’s asleep.” “It’s important.” “She’s two hundred and eleven. So is sleep.” He folds his hands around the whisky. Six fingers each, all trembling. I slide over a bowl of roasted chickpeas. “Eat something before you tell me.” “I’m not hungry.” “Excellent. They’re mostly salt.” He eats three. “My name is Pell. I’m a charter examiner for the Meridian Recovery Cooperative.” I keep polishing the glass in my hand. I have been polishing it for perhaps too long. “Salvage people,” I say. “Among other things.” “Lost cargo. Abandoned hulls.” “Disputed ownership.” A glass breaks somewhere behind me. Everyone pauses. “Gravity,” announces Brindle. “Persistent nuisance,” I say. “Brush is beside the till.” Conversation resumes. Pell doesn’t look away from me. “I’m sorry,” he says. “That’s an ambitious opening for someone who hasn’t explained himself.” He takes a wafer-thin document case from his coat. Across its lid, a silver compass turns inside a circle. I know that compass. I once wore it on my collar. I once pressed it into warm sealing wax while people packed their lives into regulation-sized boxes. Pell notices my hand stop moving. “You recognize the seal.” “Meridian puts it on everything. Hard to miss.” “This station was registered as abandoned seventeen years ago.” “Then somebody found it. That’s generally how salvage works.” “The abandonment declaration was fraudulent.” I put the glass down carefully. At table six, Ollo says, very quietly, “It’s a premium filter.” Brindle makes a sound that suggests the proposal is gaining ground. Pell opens the case. “The original owners have submitted a recovery claim. I’m required to establish occupancy, assess relocation needs, and serve notice.” “Relocation.” “Yes.” “Of thirty-eight permanent residents.” “My preliminary records say twenty-nine.” “Your preliminary records don’t count children hatched here.” His dreads draw close to his neck. “I see.” “Do you? Because I’m not sure your forms have a box for Mrs. Venn’s garden.” “I haven’t served anything yet.” I look at the document case again. “Why not?” He lowers his voice. “Because I read the passenger manifests from the other stations.” The bar feels warmer than it did a moment ago. I take away his empty bowl and replace it with stew. “That isn’t what I ordered.” “No.” “I can pay.” “I know.” He picks up the spoon. For a while, I refill drinks. I settle an argument about docking fees. I tell Brindle that crying is perfectly compatible with accepting an air filter. Then I come back. “How long?” I ask. “The recovery vessel arrives tomorrow evening.” “Quick work.” “The claim was filed eight months ago. Notices were sent.” “To where?” “The registered administrator.” “There hasn’t been an administrator here in seventeen years.” “Yes,” Pell says. “That’s one of the problems.” I lean against the counter. “Tell me the others.” “The station’s salvage title requires a witness to the original abandonment.” “It has one.” “Yes.” He touches the case. A name appears above it in pale blue letters. NETTLE VALE. I haven’t seen my surname written out in years. Usually, that feels like an achievement. Pell looks from the name to my face. “I hoped it wasn’t you.” “Why?” “Because you gave me dinner.” From the kitchen hatch, Mara says, “Nets?” She stands in her quilted dressing gown, holding the kettle. Her silver whiskers are flattened on one side. “Tell me that isn’t work.” “Go back to bed.” “Never once has that instruction preceded good news.” Pell starts to stand. “Sit,” she says. “You look like boiled laundry.” He sits. I say, “Meridian wants the station.” Mara puts the kettle down. “No.” “That was my opening position too.” “No,” she repeats, looking at me now. “You said the title was clean.” “The title passed inspection.” “That isn’t what I asked.” Between us, the beer pump clicks softly. Pell closes the document case. “There may be grounds to delay the seizure. If the witness can give a sworn account—” “No,” I say. Mara’s whiskers lift. “Nets.” “A sworn account enters the central registry. Identity confirmation. Biometrics. Employment history.” Pell says nothing. “You knew that,” I tell him. “Yes.” “And you came anyway.” “I didn’t know where else to go.” Mara studies me across the counter. Behind her, the kitchen light falls on the pencil marks where we measure the children every winter. “What happens if you testify?” she asks. I reach for the clean glass, then leave it alone. “They find me.” “Who?” Before I can answer, Pell’s case begins to chime. A small amber light pulses beneath the silver compass. He reads the message. Two of his dreads knot together. “The vessel’s changed course.” Outside, beyond the lemon tree’s reflection, a white point brightens between the rocks. Mara reaches past me and turns off the bar’s music. “How long now?” she asks.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the cozy sci-fi atmosphere requested. The author successfully establishes Nets as a compelling protagonist through her voice - dry, competent, and carrying hidden depths. Her dialogue feels natural and reveals character efficiently, particularly in exchanges like "That costs extra" / "The joke, not the whisky" which establishes her humor and practicality. The world-building is economical but effective. Details like the artificial lemon tree, heated benches for miners, and Mrs. Venn's garden create a lived-in feeling without over-explanation. The author skillfully weaves exposition into natural dialogue and action rather than dumping information. The central conflict emerges organically - Nets signed fraudulent abandonment papers seventeen years ago, making her both the key to the station's legal troubles and someone who cannot testify without exposing herself to unnamed pursuers. This creates genuine tension with no easy resolution, exactly as requested. Character interactions feel authentic, particularly the subplot with Brindle and Ollo's air filter proposal, which serves multiple purposes: establishing the community's intimacy, providing comic relief, and showing Nets' role as informal counselor. Pell is well-drawn as reluctant antagonist - his trembling hands and apologetic demeanor make him sympathetic despite his threatening mission. The pacing builds effectively toward the revelation that the recovery vessel has arrived early, ending on a cliffhanger that raises stakes without resolving the core conflict. The dialogue ratio appears close to the requested 60%. Some minor weaknesses include occasional unclear antecedents in dialogue attribution and a few moments where the prose becomes slightly precious ("the outermost dark of Andromeda"). The piece also relies somewhat heavily on withholding information about Nets' past, though this serves the mystery effectively. The writing demonstrates sophisticated understanding of character voice, efficient world-building, and natural dialogue construction. It successfully balances multiple tones - humor, tension, warmth, and foreboding - while maintaining narrative momentum. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Gone South The saxophone follows me for three blocks. Not literally. The guy playing it stays on his corner, eyes shut, one sneaker planted on his open case like he’s keeping the money from escaping. But the tune gets tangled in the crowded street, slipping between tourists and delivery carts, finding me every time I think I’ve outrun it. It sounds like somebody trying very hard not to cry. Which is obnoxious. I came two states to do that privately. At nine in the morning, New Orleans smells like hot bread, old beer, and something the sun should leave alone. My driver had dropped me beside a loading zone. “End of the line, sweetheart.” “Not your sweetheart.” He drove away before I could decide whether correcting him counted as bravery or a terminal inability to shut up. Now I have thirty-one dollars, a phone at twelve percent, and a backpack containing three shirts and absolutely no useful personality traits. Mom has called nineteen times. I turn the phone off. *** By ten, I’ve learned that looking like you know where you’re going requires actually going somewhere. I pass the same restaurant twice. On the third pass, a woman sweeping the entrance says, “You looking for somebody?” “No.” “A place, then?” “I’m exploring.” She looks at my backpack. My sweatshirt. The sweat darkening my sweatshirt. “Well, explore the shade.” She brings me a paper cup of water. This is how stupid I’ve become: kindness makes me suspicious. “Is it free?” “Water? Yes. My investment seminar costs extra.” I laugh before I can stop myself. Her name tag says **DENISE**. She points toward a public library and tells me I can sit there without buying anything. “You got somebody coming?” “Yeah,” I say. The lie comes out wearing shoes. Ready to go places. *** At the library, I find an outlet and a chair that doesn’t belong to anyone who knows me. My phone wakes up furious. **Mom: Please answer.** **Mom: You have made your point.** Then: **Mom: I need to know you’re alive.** Forty-eight hours ago, I had stood beside our refrigerator, staring at a magnet shaped like Tennessee, and said, “I’m trans.” Mom asked if the school counselor had put this in my head. Dad said we weren’t discussing it while I was “in a mood.” My sister kept eating cereal. Not because she didn’t care, maybe. Because she was eleven and the spoon was something she knew how to operate. I miss her so suddenly I feel sick. “Hey,” somebody says. “Your cord’s doing a thing.” A boot has caught my charger. The boot belongs to a kid with cropped hair, chipped green nail polish, and a denim jacket despite the heat. They untangle the cord carefully. “Sorry. Gravity’s obsessed with me.” “Tell it you need space.” They grin. “I’m Rae.” “Taylor.” “Cool. You hungry, Taylor?” Every warning I’ve ever heard crowds into my head. Rae notices. “I have crackers,” they add. “Not a van.” *** We eat outside, on a bench in the shade. Rae says they’re nineteen. I say I’m eighteen. Both lies sit between us, politely declining to introduce themselves. They’ve been here “a while.” They have a place “sometimes.” They ask whether I have somewhere tonight, and I say I’m figuring it out. “That means no,” Rae says. “So does sometimes.” Their grin disappears. For a minute, all I hear is traffic. Then Rae hands me the last cracker. “Fair.” I want to apologize. I also want them to understand that I’m not some lost little kid they can immediately understand. These desires seem inconveniently related. *** By afternoon, my backpack straps have rubbed my shoulders raw. Rae walks fast, checking behind us whenever a car slows. At a crowded corner, somebody in a spotless polo offers us money to help carry equipment. “What equipment?” I ask. “Just around back.” Rae is already moving. “Come on.” “He might’ve actually had a job.” “He might’ve.” That answer scares me worse than certainty would have. Later, when Rae ducks into a shop for water, I wait outside and wonder if they’re coming back. I could leave first. That would technically make this my decision. They return with two bottles. “You look pissed.” “I’m hot.” “You’re wearing Tennessee.” I unzip my sweatshirt. Underneath is the T-shirt I wore when I told Mom. I hate that it’s just a shirt. It ought to be smoking. *** Near evening, we stop across from a youth drop-in center Rae claims they found by accident. Someone opens the door. “Rae? We missed you yesterday.” Rae goes still. “You know her?” I ask. “No.” The woman stays in the doorway. “We saved your sketchbook.” Rae stares at the pavement. After a while, they say, “I’m seventeen.” “Sixteen.” “Yeah. You have a sixteen face.” “You have an asshole face.” Their laugh breaks halfway through. Their brother is in a different foster home. Rae left their own placement three weeks ago. They’re scared going back means being moved farther away from him. “I keep thinking I can fix it if nobody makes me leave,” they say. I look at the door. “You could’ve told me.” “I liked being somebody who knew stuff.” Across the street, the woman waits without calling again. *** Inside, there are sandwiches, mismatched chairs, and a staff member named Luis who asks what name I use. “Taylor.” “And pronouns?” “They.” He writes it down. No refrigerator hum. No Dad putting down his fork. Just a pen moving. Luis explains what he can help with, what he has to report, and what he needs to check before promising somewhere safe tonight. I don’t like all of it. I do like that he tells me. While he makes calls, Rae draws beside me, guarding the page with one elbow. I turn on my phone. **I’m alive,** I type to Mom. **I’m somewhere with staff helping me. I need you not to yell.** I don’t send the address yet. Outside, a saxophone starts up. Maybe the same guy. Maybe this city has a whole department dedicated to making people feel things against their will. My phone vibrates. I hold it facedown for one more second. Then I look.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and emotional authenticity in depicting a transgender teen's first day as a runaway in New Orleans. The writing successfully captures Taylor's voice through sharp, observational prose that balances vulnerability with defensive wit. The author skillfully employs sensory details - the persistent saxophone, the smell of "hot bread, old beer, and something the sun should leave alone" - to establish atmosphere without overindulgence. The character development is particularly strong. Taylor emerges as a complex protagonist whose defensive mechanisms (lying about age, suspicious of kindness) feel psychologically authentic for someone in their situation. The relationship with Rae develops organically, with both characters revealing layers gradually. Their mutual deception about age and the revelation of their respective circumstances creates genuine dramatic tension. The dialogue feels natural and age-appropriate, avoiding both overly mature philosophical discussions and artificially juvenile speech. Lines like "Not a van" and "You have an asshole face" capture the characters' attempts to maintain levity amid serious circumstances. The prose maintains consistent quality throughout, with memorable phrases like "The lie comes out wearing shoes. Ready to go places." The story structure follows a clear arc through Taylor's first day, hitting emotional beats effectively - from the initial disorientation through building trust with Rae to the tentative hope at the drop-in center. The ending strikes an appropriate balance, offering possibility without false resolution. Taylor's decision to text their mother but withhold the address feels earned and realistic. However, some elements feel slightly predictable - the helpful stranger, the sketchy job offer, the runaway with a tragic backstory. While executed well, these don't surprise. The pacing occasionally slows during transitional moments, though this mirrors the aimless wandering of the characters. The emotional complexity is strong but could push deeper into Taylor's internal conflict about their identity versus their family situation. The writing demonstrates professional-level craft with authentic voice work and solid character development, creating genuine engagement with Taylor's journey. + Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 78.8
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# My Apocalypse Buddy “We need water,” said Midas. “We have water,” said Chewy. “We have something that remembers water.” The bucket between them gave a small, proprietary bubble. Chewy considered it through one glass eye and one replacement shirt button. He was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from the Before, when civilisation had possessed enough electricity to waste some on reassurance. His remaining functions included waving, identifying eucalyptus, and saying *You’re doing wonderfully* at moments which suggested a sophisticated understanding of cruelty. “Today,” Midas said, “we find a pump valve. We visit the municipal works, avoid the scavengers, and come straight home.” Chewy’s left arm rose. “No questions.” “It’s a wave. The questioning mechanism fell out last winter.” *** Their home occupied a tollbooth beside a road that no longer went anywhere profitable. Midas had added a stove, a bed, and a curtain for privacy from events. He carried a crowbar, two potatoes, and Chewy in a canvas sling. The municipal works stood beyond the dead shopping precinct. Between them lay three miles of brambles, feral delivery carts, and the territory of a man who claimed to own Tuesday. It was Wednesday, according to Midas’s calendar. He had maintained Wednesday for several months. There were advantages. They reached the precinct without incident, unless one counted the incident with the goose, which Midas preferred not to. On the wall behind a gutted pharmacy, someone had painted: **WHEN THE WORLD GOES DRY** **FOLLOW THE RIVER THAT NEVER SAW SKY** **PAST THE KING WHO TAKES NO GOLD** **HOME IS UNDER WHAT YOU HOLD** Below this was a small blue leaf. “A refuge,” Midas said. “A poem,” said Chewy. “Historically, a less reliable source of drinking water.” But Midas knew the stories: hidden gardens, working wells, people who washed for reasons other than falling in. He inspected the ground. Beneath their feet, under a rusted grille, water whispered. *** The drain admitted Midas reluctantly and Chewy without comment. Midas retrieved the crowbar, which had gone ahead to investigate his ankle. They followed the underground stream by the light of Chewy’s illuminated nose. “Was that a survival feature?” Midas asked. “Bedtime comfort.” “It’s comforting.” “Please tell someone. My warranty expired during the Resource Disturbances.” The tunnel ended at a bronze king seated above a fork in the watercourse. His crown was green with corrosion. One hand extended over an inscription: **EXACT CHANGE ONLY** “The king who takes no gold,” breathed Midas. “A parking attendant,” said Chewy. Midas put a potato in the royal hand. Ancient machinery engaged. This was surprising. More surprising was the enthusiasm with which it engaged. A sluice opened behind them. Midas ran. The water ran faster, having fewer belongings. *** They emerged through a maintenance hatch in their own yard. For a while Midas lay beside the tollbooth, coughing up the river that had never seen sky. Chewy leaked through his trousers. “We have come straight home,” the koala observed. Midas looked at the tollbooth. Then at the hatch. Then at the blue leaf scratched into its underside. “Home is under what you hold.” “You hold several mistaken assumptions.” “The tollbooth was part of the waterworks.” This explained the pipes beneath the floor, which Midas had assumed were for tolls. He fetched a shovel. *** Under the bed, under the floorboards, and under a layer of previous occupants’ regrettable decisions, they found a steel door. It had a handwheel. Midas turned it. Nothing happened. He applied the crowbar. Something happened to the crowbar. Chewy watched him sit down. “The other direction,” he suggested. Beyond the door, stairs descended into warm, damp darkness. At their foot stood rows of pale plants beneath shafts of daylight. Water trickled through stone channels. A refuge. Also six people holding agricultural implements with a distinctly non-agricultural attitude. Their leader was a narrow woman wearing a necklace of tap washers. “You’ve opened the upper sluice,” she said. “Technically,” said Midas, “a potato did.” “Reservoir’s draining into the overflow. Another hour and we lose the garden.” Midas looked at the lettuces. They were the first he had seen that weren’t illustrations. “Can it be stopped?” “From the roof.” *** The roof belonged to a pumping tower half a mile away, reached by an overgrown service track through the wilds. The woman, whose name was Vale, gave Midas a wrench. “Why me?” “You’re the right weight.” “For what?” But she had become busy pointing. At the tower, Midas discovered a counterweighted inspection cradle. Its cable crossed the valley toward the tollbooth. Chewy examined the mechanism. “Good news. No electricity required.” “What’s the bad news?” “No brakes required, apparently.” Midas climbed anyway. Below him the wilds shifted in the wind: birches through asphalt, fox paths through offices, a forest patiently repossessing a conference centre. At the top, he found the emergency valve. It resisted the wrench. He added the crowbar. The valve surrendered. So did the platform. *** The cradle carried them home at a speed Midas considered personally insulting. It struck the tollbooth roof, passed through it, and settled on the bed. Silence followed, interrupted by the slow arrival of roofing material. Chewy’s waving arm lay in Midas’s lap. “You’re doing wonderfully,” he said. Midas laughed until he discovered which rib objected. *** By evening the reservoir had stabilised. Vale offered them a dry corner below, meals, and work repairing the damage. Midas accepted before she could develop the offer further. He carried down his blankets, stove, and surviving potato. Last came the tollbooth door. “You don’t need that,” Vale said. “It’s my front door.” “There’s no wall.” “I’ve had a difficult day. I’d like to keep one architectural principle.” He propped it beside their new sleeping place. Chewy sat on the blankets while Midas stitched his arm back on. Above them, wind moved through the ruined tollbooth. Below, clean water kept its own counsel. “Successful mission?” Midas asked. “We found a valve.” “We lost the house.” “Only the outside.” Midas shut the door carefully. It fell over. Neither of them felt obliged to discuss it.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates a strong grasp of Terry Pratchett's distinctive style, capturing his dry wit, absurdist logic, and philosophical undertones wrapped in seemingly simple adventure narrative. The author successfully creates a post-apocalyptic world that feels both desolate and oddly whimsical, where civilization's remnants take on new, often ironic purposes. The characterization is particularly effective. Midas emerges as a believably hapless protagonist whose misfortunes feel both inevitable and endearing. His practical concerns ("We need water") contrasted with his tendency toward romantic interpretation of clues creates authentic character tension. Chewy, the animatronic koala, serves as an excellent foil - his programmed responses like "You're doing wonderfully" at inappropriate moments capture Pratchett's talent for finding humor in dysfunction. The prose style successfully mimics Pratchett's economy of language and deadpan delivery. Lines like "The bucket between them gave a small, proprietary bubble" and "He fetched a shovel" demonstrate the author's understanding of how Pratchett builds humor through understatement and matter-of-fact descriptions of absurd situations. The plot structure adheres well to the prompt's requirements, beginning with deliberation, proceeding through escalating mishaps, and returning the characters home "worse for wear" but oddly better off. The mission does indeed go sideways in multiple ways - the simple search for a pump valve leads to underground chases, mechanical disasters, and architectural destruction. However, the piece occasionally lacks the deeper philosophical resonance that elevates Pratchett's best work. While it captures his surface humor effectively, it doesn't quite achieve the layered meaning that makes his writing memorable beyond its comedic value. The dialogue, while functional, could be sharper and more distinctive between characters. The imagery is generally strong, particularly in descriptions of the post-apocalyptic landscape: "birches through asphalt, fox paths through offices, a forest patiently repossessing a conference centre." These details effectively establish the world without over-explaining. The ending strikes an appropriate balance - the characters have lost their home but gained something potentially better, though the author wisely avoids making this transformation feel too neat or unearned. The final image of the door falling over and neither character feeling "obliged to discuss it" perfectly captures the resigned pragmatism that defines both characters. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The man who fell through Nia’s door brought rain, a gust of March wind, and the unmistakable sound of somebody outside shouting, “Rhys! Over here!” “Lock that,” he said. “Good afternoon to you, too.” “Please lock that.” Nia turned the key. Through the rippled glass, three figures hurried past towards the bridge. The man bent double beside Welsh History. “If you’re sick,” she said, “aim for the bucket. Not the Tudors.” He looked up, breathing hard. Even upside down, Rhys Vaughan had the face currently occupying half the bus shelters in Wales. “You recognise me.” “You’re standing on Owain Glyndŵr.” He lifted his boot from a fallen paperback. “Sorry.” “To him, not me.” Rhys retrieved it. “Owain. Terrible business. Big admirer of your work.” Nia took the book before she could laugh. “Are they gone?” “For now.” “Marvellous. You’ve saved my life.” “Then buy something. We’ve had a slow Thursday.” He straightened, adjusting his wet coat. It was almost visible, the moment he arranged himself: shoulders loose, smile crooked, one eyebrow suggesting they shared an excellent secret. “What would you recommend?” “A less conspicuous coat.” “It was a gift.” “From someone who wanted you found?” This time his laugh sounded unprepared. He glanced around the shop: the bowed shelves, the little stove, the handwritten notice asking customers not to feed the cat. “Beautiful place.” “Thank you.” “Beautiful owner.” “No returns on that one, I’m afraid.” His smile faltered. Nia busied herself aligning bookmarks. Her fingers had become absurdly unhelpful. She had watched him kiss somebody against a lighthouse wall on television last Sunday and had needed to open a window afterwards. “Too much?” he asked. “By several inches.” “I can start again.” “The door sticks. Give it a shoulder.” “You’re enjoying this.” “A slow Thursday, as I said.” He walked towards the counter, then stopped at the respectable distance she had silently demanded. “I’m Rhys.” “I gathered.” “And you are?” “Working.” His mouth twitched, but his eyes searched her face. “Have I actually annoyed you?” The question arrived without polish. Nia looked down at the bookmarks, now arranged with the precision of surgical instruments. “Not actually.” “Oh.” He exhaled. “Good.” Outside, a camera flashed against the glass. Nia caught his sleeve and pulled him behind the tall display of local walks. “Down.” “I usually require dinner first.” “Keep talking and I’ll fetch him a chair.” Rhys crouched. Nia stood close enough to smell rain in his hair and something expensive beneath it. Her hand remained on his sleeve a moment too long. A shadow paused at the door. “We’re closed,” she called. The letterbox rattled. “Just want a picture, love.” “Then there’s a lovely bridge. Been there for centuries. Very patient.” The shadow lingered, then moved away. Rhys looked up at her. “That was magnificent.” “That was customer service.” “I think I’m in love.” “I think you’re frightened.” His expression changed so quickly she wished she could retrieve the words. Then he sat on the floor. “Yes,” he said. “Well. Both make me talk rubbish.” Nia lowered herself onto the stool beside the display. Her knees felt unreliable. “Why Crickhowell?” “My sister lives outside town. New baby. I came to be the glamorous uncle.” “And?” “He vomited down my neck. Apparently he prefers my earlier work.” “Discerning child.” “I thought a walk might improve my reception.” “You could stop trying to be received.” He picked at a loose thread on his cuff. “Could I?” The stove ticked. Nia waited. She knew how to leave silence alone; people bought books partly for that. “When I was nine,” he said, “I played the innkeeper in the school nativity. One line. ‘There’s no room.’ My mother was in the front row, laughing with her friend.” “At you?” “No. That was the problem. Not looking at me at all.” His thumbnail caught the thread again. “So I added a joke about the stable having en-suite facilities. Brought the house down. Then another joke. Then I offered Joseph breakfast.” Nia laughed before she could stop herself. “There,” he said softly. “What?” “That. I’ve been doing it ever since.” She watched his hand go still. “What happened to the play?” “Mary hit me with the baby Jesus.” “Fair enough.” “Very fair.” He looked towards the window. “I remember the teacher taking me aside afterwards. I kept making her laugh while she told me off. Couldn’t bear her being cross with me.” “And now?” “Now people get paid to tell me I’m delightful. Makes it difficult to check.” Nia rubbed her thumb over a rough place on the stool. “You’ve bent the cover of a twelve-pound walking guide.” He looked down, horrified. “Oh, hell.” “But you put Glyndŵr back.” “Some hope for me, then?” “Limited.” His smile returned, smaller this time. She liked it much more, which was inconvenient. “What’s your name?” he asked. “Nia.” “Nia.” He said it without doing anything clever to it. “Would you choose me a book?” “What do you like?” “I was about to say whatever you like.” “Were you?” “Appalling, isn’t it?” “A bit.” “Something quiet,” he said. “No one being murdered for once.” She stood and fetched a slim novel from the shelf behind him. “This.” He read the back carefully. She pretended not to watch. “I’ll take it. And the injured walking guide.” At the till, their fingers touched over his card. Nia entered the wrong amount and had to cancel it. Rhys noticed. Mercifully, he said nothing. “There’s a back door,” she told him. “Through the yard. Turn left by the bins.” “Your VIP entrance?” “Only the finest bins.” He tucked the books inside his coat. “Could I come back?” “It’s a shop.” “Right.” He looked down, then tried again. “Could I come back when I don’t need hiding?” Nia slipped his receipt into the novel. “Tell me what you think of that first.” “What if I hate it?” “Then we’ll have something to discuss.” At the back door he paused, smiling. Nia held it open, letting in the rain. “Mind the bins,” she said.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong craft in several key areas while maintaining the requested romantic tension and character dynamics. The author successfully creates two distinct voices - Rhys's performative charm gradually giving way to vulnerability, and Nia's dry wit masking her own attraction. The Welsh setting feels authentic without being heavy-handed, and the dialogue carries the scene effectively as requested. The characterization is particularly well-executed. Rhys embodies the "rogue with fragile ego" perfectly - his automatic charm offensive ("Beautiful owner") immediately deflated by Nia's sharp responses, leading to genuine moments of vulnerability like his childhood nativity story. Nia's character is equally well-drawn, her surface immunity to his charm believably undermined by small physical tells (fumbling bookmarks, unreliable knees, entering the wrong amount at the till). The dialogue feels natural and serves multiple purposes - advancing the plot, revealing character, and building romantic tension. Lines like "You're standing on Owain Glyndŵr" and "No returns on that one, I'm afraid" showcase Nia's wit while "I think I'm in love" / "I think you're frightened" captures the emotional core of their dynamic. The pacing works well, moving from comedy through tension to genuine connection. The nativity story serves as an effective turning point where Rhys drops his performance, and Nia's response shows her growing attraction despite herself. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the wit feels slightly forced, and the ending, while charming, edges toward predictable romantic comedy territory. The piece also relies heavily on dialogue with less attention to sensory details beyond the essential setting elements. The prose style is clean and controlled, avoiding purple language while maintaining elegance. The author shows rather than tells the growing attraction through physical details and behavioral changes rather than explicit statements. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door yielded before Aya touched it. That was the first wrong thing. The second was the smell: not the bitter incense that fed the wards, but hot whale oil and somebody’s excellent tobacco. “Don’t,” Simeon whispered. They were already across the threshold. Six lamps burned beneath green glass shades. Their light caught on the iron ribs of the ceiling, the sweating brickwork, the shallow drainage channels cut into the floor. At the far end of the underhold, where the Scythan artifact ought to have stood behind its lattice of consecrated wire, a woman sat in a leather chair. Mother Vey wore her black churchgoing dress. Across her knees rested a double-barrelled boarding pistol, its brasswork polished bright as wedding gold. “Shut the door, Katra,” she said. “You’re letting the warmth out.” Katra stopped with one boot still on the threshold. “Morning, Mother.” “It has been.” Two men stood behind the chair. Others occupied the dark between the lamps. Aya recognised Brannick by his jaw, rebuilt in steel after a dockside accident. His companion held a cocked arbalest, the bolt aimed at Simeon’s stomach. No one shouted. That frightened Aya more than shouting would have. “We heard you’d been taken,” she said. Behind her mask, her voice sounded almost ordinary. “So you came to fetch my property.” “To keep it safe.” Mother Vey tapped ash into a silver dish. “From whom?” Katra’s fingers twitched beside her coat. “Hands on your head, love,” Vey told her. “You’ve a knife in each sleeve and another down your stocking. Don’t oblige Mr Brannick to be thorough.” Katra obeyed. Simeon raised his hands without instruction. His spectacles had slipped down his nose; he looked absurdly like a clerk surprised at luncheon. “I said the wards were wrong,” he murmured. “You said they were dormant,” Aya answered. “Yes. Well. Educational distinction.” From the harbour beyond the guild walls, a distant foghorn sounded three times. The last note seemed to linger inside the stone. Aya reached inward, towards the cold place behind her thoughts. Something stirred there. It had no face until she remembered faces. Then it wore her mother’s, swollen above the rope. The lamps guttered. Mother Vey lifted the pistol. “Not another inch.” A pressure closed around Aya’s skull. She saw the black nails driven through the doorframe, each capped with a milk tooth. Wards. Not removed. Reversed. The thing behind her thoughts pressed nearer, hungry for the opening she could no longer give it. “Clever girl,” Vey said. “You’ve noticed.” Brannick took Aya’s wrists. She let him. His hands were warm, calloused, almost gentle as he closed an iron cuff around each one. A little oil leaked from his jaw onto her shoulder. Katra watched him with naked hatred. “Easy on her.” “Still giving orders?” Vey asked. “Still got a mouth.” “For the present.” They were searched and bound beneath the lamps. Simeon surrendered two lock picks, a folding voltmeter and a packet of indigestion powders. Katra’s knives made a neat, accusing row. From Aya, Brannick took a silver lancet. Then he reached for her mask. “No,” she said. It escaped her too quickly. Too plainly. Mother Vey leaned forward. “Ah.” Aya tried to hold herself still as the ribbons loosened. The mask came away with a faint pull against the damp skin beneath her eyes. For a moment there was only the ticking of cooling lamp fittings. Then Simeon said, very softly, “Oh, hell.” Vey studied her. “Lady Aya.” Her name sounded indecent in that room. “Your father opened the new customs house last winter. I watched him cut the ribbon.” Aya could see it already: the breakfast papers; her father’s secretary carrying them away; servants looking down as she passed. Her mother’s portrait had disappeared in just that fashion. First from the drawing room, then from the house. At the trial they had called her mother’s curiosity a moral defect. Aya had been nine. “Did you know?” Vey asked the others. “Never asked,” Katra said. “An admirable principle in our profession.” “I knew she had money,” Simeon said. “I assumed a regrettable uncle.” Vey smiled without warmth. “The watch took a woman from my bed this morning. Veil, nightdress, suitable screaming. By noon she’ll be released for want of evidence.” “You baited us,” Aya said. “I left something unattended. You supplied the rest.” Beside Vey’s chair stood a narrow iron casket. Through its open lid Aya glimpsed the artifact: a curve of white material, neither bone nor metal, pierced with holes that seemed deeper than the object itself. She looked away before they arranged themselves into eyes. “You needn’t kill us,” she said. “Need is a high threshold.” “My father will pay.” “He might pay for your silence. That’s not quite the same transaction.” “He’ll pay for my return.” “After I tell him where you’ve been? What you’ve been doing?” Aya swallowed. She had imagined discovery as an argument: doors slammed, allowances stopped, a carriage waiting to take her somewhere dreary. Not the magistrate who had sentenced her mother taking tea with her father. “Then don’t tell him everything.” Vey waited. “You have his daughter,” Aya continued. “Keep her respectable. Keep her frightened. Ask for money first.” “And afterwards?” “Customs schedules. Inspection warrants. Things he can obtain without admitting why.” Katra turned towards her. “Aya—” “All three of us live,” Aya said. “Or you lose my cooperation.” Mother Vey considered her, then gestured at Brannick. “Separate rooms. Feed them.” Relief hurt worse than the cuffs. As Brannick led her away, Vey spoke again. “Your mother offered services, too.” Aya stopped. Vey closed the casket. “We’ll discuss her mistakes tomorrow.” Beyond the door, something wearing her mother’s face began to laugh.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and atmospheric worldbuilding within the whalepunk fantasy setting. The author successfully creates a tense confrontation scene that adheres closely to the prompt's requirements, incorporating all requested story beats while maintaining consistent characterization and voice. The prose style effectively captures the requested gritty Victorian aesthetic with gothic horror elements. Descriptions like "iron ribs of the ceiling" and "sweating brickwork" establish the industrial atmosphere, while details such as Brannick's steel jaw and the reversed wards create an appropriately dark, mechanical-magical world. The dialogue feels authentic to the setting, with characters speaking in clipped, period-appropriate exchanges that reveal personality and tension. Character work is particularly strong. Aya's internal conflict between her aristocratic identity and criminal activities creates genuine emotional stakes. Her desperation when unmasked feels earned, and her attempt to negotiate using her social position demonstrates both intelligence and moral compromise. Mother Vey emerges as a formidable antagonist through economical characterization - her calm control and strategic thinking make her genuinely threatening without requiring exposition. The pacing builds tension effectively, moving from the ominous quiet entrance through the revelation of Vey's presence to Aya's unmasking and desperate negotiation. The magical elements are well-integrated, with Aya's connection to "immateria" feeling both powerful and constrained by the world's rules. The reversed wards provide a clever plot device that demonstrates Vey's cunning while limiting Aya's options. Some minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the prose becomes slightly overwrought ("something wearing her mother's face began to laugh"), though these don't significantly detract from the overall effectiveness. The ending strikes an appropriately dark note without feeling gratuitously grim, setting up future conflict while resolving the immediate scene's tension. The piece successfully avoids common pitfalls like unearned character transformations or incongruous tonal shifts. The dialogue serves multiple functions - advancing plot, revealing character, and maintaining atmosphere - without feeling forced or expository.
