Through the kitchen window he saw Mike at the stove. His father sat at the table. Opposite him sat a boy in JT’s red hunting jacket. JT looked down. He was wearing the same jacket. The same little burn above the pocket. Inside, the boy raised his head. His father followed the boy’s gaze and saw JT at the window. For a moment neither moved. I can’t write in Neil Gaiman’s exact style, but here’s an original story blending dry dark fantasy, infernal bureaucracy, and domestic absurdity. # Hell Is Other Demons At seven, Lucifer discovered that his throne had developed a list to the left. At seven-oh-three, he discovered why. “Drop it.” The hellhound looked up. Between its jaws was a length of wrought iron ending in a decorative hoof. “Now.” Biscuits swallowed. Lucifer stood in his dressing gown and considered the limitations of absolute power. From beneath the breakfast table came a small, metallic belch. *** Lilith arrived at eight carrying a paper bag. “I was passing.” “You live beyond the gates of uncreation.” “There’s a bakery.” She put the bag on the table. Two pastries. One without almonds. Lucifer decided not to notice. They had been separated for eleven months, or six thousand years, depending on which department handled the paperwork. Her official forwarding address was NONE OF YOUR BUSINESS, a jurisdiction recently recognized by the Infernal Postal Union. “Your chair’s crooked,” she said. “It’s a throne.” “Then your throne’s crooked.” Biscuits emerged from beneath the table, wagging the part of his tail that wasn’t fire. Lilith scratched behind his central ear. “You encourage him,” Lucifer said. “He needs stimulation.” “He ate a duke yesterday.” “Was the duke interesting?” *** At nine they attended the daily suffering review. Lilith wasn’t meant to attend. She had come to collect a silver hairpin, although Lucifer was fairly certain she had collected it last Thursday. The minister for inventive punishments presented his quarterly figures. “We’ve introduced an arrangement for dishonest landlords. Their victims control the temperature.” “Effective?” asked Lucifer. “Extremely. We’re having trouble retaining maintenance staff.” “Approve it.” Lilith leafed through the agenda. “You’re still tormenting adulterers in the western furnaces?” “It’s traditional.” “Half of them arrived here because they fell in love with somebody inconvenient.” “Some of them lied.” “Yes,” she said. “People do.” The minister looked down at his figures with professional intensity. Lucifer crossed out the item. “Fraud division can assess them individually.” “Very humane,” said Lilith. “I’m streamlining.” Under the table, Biscuits began eating a ceremonial spur. *** At eleven, a delegation of demons requested permission to revolt. Their leader, a flayed accountant named Vassago, laid out a proposal in duplicate. “We feel the current administration lacks direction.” “Our direction is down.” “With respect, Your Darkness, that’s geography.” Lucifer signed the authorization. “Thursday. No weapons in the kitchens. Last time someone perforated the refrigerator.” Vassago hesitated. “And the reprisals?” “Standard.” “Families included?” “Immediate only.” The delegation withdrew, reasonably satisfied. Lilith watched them go. “You used to enjoy crushing insurrections.” “I used to have weekends.” “You never had weekends.” “I used to have you.” It escaped before he could improve it. Lilith examined a stain on her sleeve. “You had me,” she said, “and you had a remarkable talent for being elsewhere.” From the throne room came the grinding shriek of enamel against iron. Lucifer closed his eyes. *** Lunch was in the little kitchen behind the Hall of Irrevocable Verdicts. They had once entertained there. Lilith had cooked; Lucifer had selected wines and taken credit for the atmosphere. Now the cupboards contained mustard, several excellent poisons, and a jar of olives old enough to qualify as witnesses. “You’re not eating properly,” she said. “I don’t require nourishment.” “You don’t require that dressing gown either.” He looked down. One cuff was scorched. She made eggs. He stood beside her, wanting to help and knowing that asking where the pans were would establish several things neither of them needed established. “I could set the table.” “Good.” He laid two places. After a moment, he took away the third fork. Lilith noticed but said nothing. The fork had been for nobody. He sometimes made mistakes like that now. *** At two, the throne collapsed during a sentencing. Lucifer dropped approximately eighteen inches and landed among the severed legs of his office. The condemned man, a pharmaceutical executive, laughed. The court became very quiet. “That,” Lucifer said from the floor, “is going to affect your placement.” Biscuits bounded forward, delighted that his master had finally joined the game. Lilith covered her mouth. “Don’t,” Lucifer warned. “I’m not.” Her shoulders shook. The pharmaceutical executive, encouraged by what he tragically misread as solidarity, laughed again. *** By four, the palace carpenter had declared the throne repairable but emotionally significant. “You don’t usually say that about furniture,” Lucifer said. “New training requirement, sire.” The carpenter recommended bitter spray. “It discourages chewing.” “Will it work on a hellhound?” “No guarantee. Could try giving him something he’s allowed to destroy.” Lucifer glanced at the waiting room. “Not a petitioner,” said Lilith. “You’ve become very particular.” She removed her coat. Together they dragged a condemned torture rack into the courtyard. Biscuits attacked it with immediate conviction. For twenty minutes, they watched him reduce a major instrument of state policy to kindling. “He missed you,” Lucifer said. “He’s a dog.” “Yes.” “You could have called.” “You said not to.” “I said not to call and explain why I was wrong.” Lucifer watched Biscuits shake a leather restraint triumphantly. “That did limit my options.” Lilith laughed, once, despite herself. *** At six, the sun failed to set, as usual. Lilith found her hairpin in the pocket of her coat. Neither mentioned it. Lucifer poured wine. Beyond the balcony, the damned labored beneath overseers who were themselves subject to increasingly elaborate performance reviews. “I’m not moving back,” she said. “I didn’t ask.” “You put my cup out.” “It’s a cup.” “It says *World’s Worst Mother*.” “The children chose it.” “You coached them.” “They struggled with the apostrophe.” She accepted the wine. They stood close enough for their sleeves to touch. *** At ten, Lilith left. She kissed his cheek, briefly enough to permit later disagreement about its meaning. “Get the throne fixed.” “It’s being done.” “And walk him.” “He has the courtyard.” “Walk him, Lucifer.” After she had gone, he found a toothbrush beside his in the bathroom. He didn’t touch it. Instead, he fetched the lead. Biscuits came skidding down the corridor, scattering sparks, carrying the carpenter’s left boot. “No,” said Lucifer. The hellhound dropped it. For a moment, Lucifer simply stared. Then he clipped on the lead and took the creature out among the screams.

+ Historical fiction: Gladiator — Score: 88.7
Prompt:
Historical Fiction: Write a scene from a story set during the height of the Roman Empire, focusing on a slice of a day in the life of a gladiator. Do not write a combat scene. Use sensory details to capture the sights, sounds, and smells of ancient Rome. Explore the gladiator's thoughts and emotions. The story should also touch on the larger political and social issues of the time period. The piece should feel like a slice of a larger story. First person, past tense, 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the time the sun reached the upper windows of the Ludus Magnus, I had washed another man's blood from my tunic. It was not much: a rust-colored thumbprint left by the physician, who had examined my shoulder before breakfast. The water in the basin smelled of iron and yesterday's onions. Beyond the wall, a cart wheel shrieked against its axle, and someone cursed a mule with the patient inventiveness of a man who expected no improvement. I wrung the cloth carefully. My left arm still resisted anything above the waist. The physician had called this fortunate: nothing broken, nothing that required an expensive remedy. He spoke of my body as the stablemen spoke of horses, with genuine concern governed by arithmetic. I had learned to be grateful for that concern. A horse worth saving at least received clean straw. Across the courtyard, Felix sat on an overturned bucket, threading a needle through the strap of his sandal. He had been born in Rome and had sold his freedom to pay debts. This seemed to me a stranger custom than anything our conquerors attributed to Dacia. When I had asked him why, he had said that freedom without bread was merely permission to starve in any doorway you pleased. That morning he held the sandal against the light and swore at it. “Your god has wings on his feet,” he said. “Ask him for better leather.” Above my sleeping shelf stood a little Mercury, molded in clay, with one wing chipped away. A cook had given him to me after I found her missing knife. I had kept him because he watched over travelers and thieves, and I could not decide which profession my survival required. At home my father had prayed to other powers. None of their names had helped him when the granaries burned. I touched the god's clay head with a damp finger. I had no wine to offer him. Carry a message, I thought. Only that. Gods who demanded cattle belonged to men who owned them. At midday the laundry woman came through the service gate, bent beneath a basket that seemed larger than her ribs. Her name was Tertia. She brought the smell of damp wool, stale urine, and the street: hot bread, dung, a sweetness of bruised figs. The porter lifted her bundles with a stick. He enjoyed discovering contraband, though he enjoyed being paid not to discover it still more. Tertia complained loudly about a missing sheet. When she reached me, she laid a folded tunic beside the basin. Her hands were red and cracked along the knuckles. “Yours,” she said. The cloth was warm from her shoulder. Inside its fold lay a narrow strip of blue wool, tied with three knots. My sister had tied knots that way when she wanted to mark something as hers: a basket, a lamb, my sleeve when we were children and she feared losing me in a crowd. For a moment I heard nothing, although the city continued making its enormous noise. Then the water dripping from my tunic struck the basin once, twice, and sound returned with such force that I nearly dropped the wool. “Where?” I asked. Tertia rubbed her nose with her wrist. “A house on the Aventine. She works the loom. That's all I could learn without questions being asked about me.” Alive was not a place. I wanted a doorway, a name, the number of steps between us. Yet alive was more than I had possessed that morning, and my knees weakened under the weight of it. I gripped the basin's rim. Tertia looked away, giving me that small privacy. Behind her, steam lifted from the kitchen roof; somebody was boiling lentils with garlic, enough garlic to disguise almost anything. “Did she ask for me?” “She asked whether you still sang.” I had forgotten that I had ever sung. I remembered suddenly the words to a song about a fox stealing cheese, and my mother's voice interrupting mine because I always gave away the ending. I pressed the wool into my palm until the knots hurt. The porter called Tertia back. She left me before I could ask what answer she had given. Outside, trumpets announced some procession I could not see. Rome was still celebrating the emperor's victory, as though Dacia could be conquered afresh each afternoon. Gold from our mountains paid for spectacles; men from our villages supplied them. Felix said the people loved Trajan because he fed them and built things. I believed him. From the gate I had once watched a boy lick spilled grain from his fingers. I doubted he cared which province had paid for it. Felix came over when the porter turned away. I showed him the wool. He did not make a joke, which frightened me more than anything he might have said. “A household slave can sometimes be bought,” he said. “With what?” He glanced toward the offices, where the clerk kept our accounts and recorded the gifts admirers sent us. Somewhere in those tablets lay the price of my shoulder, my meals, perhaps my sister. I hated him for making hope sound like bookkeeping. That afternoon I was meant to mend the padding of my helmet. Instead I sat beside Felix and watched him draw his needle through the leather. He offered to speak to a man who carried messages for the wealthy spectators. I knew what such favors cost, though I had never paid for one. Across the yard, the clerk opened his shutters. I saw the pale square of his face above the dark sill, and then the little scales on his desk. Before I rose, I tucked the blue wool inside my tunic, against the skin beneath my injured shoulder. Mercury could keep his winged sandals; I needed only to cross the courtyard. Still, I looked toward my cell and promised him wine. Then I asked Felix to come with me, because fear always spoiled my careful Latin.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates sophisticated historical fiction writing with strong adherence to the prompt requirements. The author successfully creates an immersive slice-of-life scene set in ancient Rome, focusing on a Dacian gladiator's daily experience without resorting to combat sequences. The sensory details are expertly woven throughout - the iron smell of bloody water mixed with onions, the shriek of cart wheels, the scent of damp wool and street life that the laundry woman brings. These details create authentic atmosphere without feeling forced or excessive. The characterization is nuanced and believable. The protagonist emerges as a complex individual - a conquered Dacian processing trauma, loss, and unexpected hope. His relationship with Felix provides natural exposition about Roman social structures, particularly the concept of voluntary slavery for debt relief. The protagonist's observations about freedom versus survival feel authentic to someone from his background. The prose style is elegant and controlled, with a voice that feels appropriately reflective for the character and time period. Sentences flow naturally with varied rhythm and structure. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining literary quality. The emotional core - discovering his sister is alive - provides genuine stakes and complexity. The protagonist's reaction feels earned and realistic, from the momentary disorientation to the practical considerations of what this knowledge means. Historical and social elements are seamlessly integrated. The references to Trajan's Dacian campaigns, the social hierarchy, economic realities of gladiatorial life, and religious syncretism all feel researched and authentic rather than superficial. The ending maintains appropriate emotional weight without false optimism. The protagonist faces difficult choices with uncertain outcomes, which feels true to his circumstances. Minor weaknesses include some dialogue that, while functional, could be more distinctive. The pacing occasionally slows during exposition, though this doesn't significantly detract from engagement. + Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Skerryvore Lighthouse, 6 September 1962** Mam, Arrived yesterday with my bag and the tin you said would keep biscuits dry. It keeps wet socks damp equally well. You should see the stonework. Every block fitted into the next, and the whole tower standing where you’d swear nothing could stand. Tiree shows to the northeast when the weather allows. There are three of us. Bell is principal keeper. Fraser has photographs of six children tucked behind his clock. My first pay should reach you Friday. Keep the extra. Love, Alec --- **Glasgow, 12 September 1962** Dear Alec, Your money came. I have put the extra aside, since you have apparently become the Bank of Scotland. Do not dry socks in a biscuit tin. I expect this is a joke but with you it is difficult to tell. Mrs Kerr asked whether you climb outside to light it. I said you are a trained man with electrical equipment, though I would appreciate confirmation. The factory is on short time. Nothing to concern yourself about. Love, Mam --- **Skerryvore, 28 October 1962** Mam, Electric lamp, yes. Tell Mrs Kerr I strike a match off a passing gull. We polish more than we repair. Salt gets everywhere. Bell can find a thumbprint in the dark. Relief was cancelled twice. I’d packed before the first cancellation, which Fraser says you never do. Now I leave everything out and pretend that means something. Send news of your street. Who’s moved, who’s quarrelling. Anything with people walking about in it. Alec --- **Glasgow, 4 November 1962** Dear Alec, Number twelve has a new baby called Gordon. The father wanted Elvis. That is the standard of dispute available here. I went to your room for the scarf you requested. There was a saucer beneath the bed containing three screws and a tooth. Please explain only the tooth. You need not send more because of the short time. I am managing. Do you get outside every day? I don’t like thinking of those stairs being your whole walk. Mam --- **Skerryvore, 19 December 1962** Mam, The tooth came out when I was twelve. You said the dentist might need it. Outside depends on the sea. Sometimes we open the door and shut it again. I’m sorry leave was poor. I’d things to tell you, then couldn’t think of them with the wireless on. I wasn’t annoyed about the factory. Back here the sound never stops. Even in bed I’m listening for a change in it. Bell says I’ll learn which noises matter. Christmas money enclosed. Buy yourself something that isn’t coal. Love, Alec --- **Glasgow, 27 December 1962** Dear Alec, I bought coal. You may report me. Your scarf missed the boat, according to the office. It is coming with the next stores. I unravelled the tight end and did it again. You asked if I was still doing Thursdays. There are no Thursdays now. They closed our floor in November. I didn’t tell you at Christmas because you were sleeping so badly. There is the unemployment money. I have worked twenty-six years; I am entitled to it. Mam --- **Skerryvore, 14 January 1963** Mam, Why did you let me talk about buying a motorbike? I’ve asked the office to increase your allotment. Don’t argue. It’s not as if there’s a pub here. Fraser went home and his replacement whistles through his teeth. A decent fellow. I find myself waiting for him to start, then being angry before he does. Yesterday I cleaned the same contact twice because I couldn’t remember doing it. No harm done. I checked everything afterwards. Don’t mention that to anyone. Alec --- **Glasgow, 22 January 1963** Dear Alec, I let you talk about a motorbike because you wanted a motorbike. Being out of work does not require everyone else to stop wanting things. I have used some of your money. Rent, mostly. I was embarrassed after my grand speech about putting it aside. You sound tired in a way sleep isn’t sorting. Tell Bell about the contact. You would tell him if another man had done it. Give yourself the same consideration. Love, Mam --- **Skerryvore, 3 March 1963** Mam, I told him. He checked the work and changed the watches. The doctor on Tiree says I should ask for shore work. There may be something at the Oban depot, but nothing promised. Less money. I keep taking the application out. There’s nothing difficult on it. Name, service, reasons. I like the machinery. When a fault makes sense, I can work all day. Then supper comes and there are another fourteen hours before morning. I don’t know what to write under reasons. Alec --- **Glasgow, 10 March 1963** Dear Alec, Write what you wrote to me. I have asked about a smaller place. Before you object, half this house is furniture I dust because nobody uses it. Your allotment has helped me. I am grateful. That doesn’t make staying there your obligation. Send the application. You can come here while they decide. I’ll turn the wireless off. Mam --- **Skerryvore, 16 March 1963** Mam, Application sent. I cried when Bell signed it. Not much, but enough that we both had to wait. He gave me his handkerchief and asked whether I wanted him to post it with the station papers. I said yes. I’ve been trying not to disappoint you. It occurs to me I haven’t asked what actually would. Alec --- **Oban, 8 June 1963** Dear Alec, Home safely. You needn’t meet every train I’m on. Your workshop suits you. I liked seeing the dismantled lamps laid out, and you explaining what each piece did without apologising for being interested. I accept the little room, if your landlady still agrees. The stairs are manageable. We will keep separate purses. Bring my sewing machine when you come Saturday. Leave the big wardrobe. I’m pleased you’ll be there. Love, Mam
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary narrative successfully captures the voice of a working-class Scottish lighthouse keeper through restrained, authentic correspondence with his mother. The author demonstrates strong technical control over the format, creating two distinct voices that feel genuine and lived-in. Alec's letters are spare and observational, often deflecting emotion through dry humor, while his mother's responses show practical wisdom and understated affection. The story builds tension effectively through accumulating details about isolation's psychological toll. The progression from mundane observations about biscuit tins and socks to Alec's admission of memory lapses and crying feels organic rather than forced. The author avoids melodrama, instead letting the emotional weight emerge through small, telling details like the saved tooth or the repeated cleaning of the same contact. The Scottish working-class voices are convincingly rendered without resorting to heavy dialect or stereotypes. Phrases like "I expect this is a joke but with you it is difficult to tell" and "You may report me" capture the characters' personalities and relationship dynamics efficiently. The mother's voice particularly shines in her blend of practicality and concern. The setting comes alive through sensory details - salt getting everywhere, the constant sound of the sea, the precision required for lighthouse maintenance. These elements serve the story rather than overwhelming it. The author shows admirable restraint in description, letting the lighthouse's isolation speak through its effects on the characters rather than through overwrought atmospheric writing. The emotional climax - Alec's breakdown when Bell signs his transfer application - feels earned after months of accumulated stress. The resolution, with both characters finding new living arrangements and Alec transitioning to shore work, provides closure without false optimism. The final letter's warmth ("I'm pleased you'll be there") feels genuine rather than artificially uplifting. Minor weaknesses include some moments where the period setting could be more firmly established, and occasionally the Scottish dialect feels slightly inconsistent. However, these are small flaws in an otherwise accomplished piece that demonstrates sophisticated understanding of character development and narrative pacing within the constraints of the epistolary form. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 81.8
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The restaurant has three exits, two cameras, and a reservation tablet angled toward the room. I notice those before I notice her earrings. This is not a charming fact about me. Her earrings are tiny swords. I notice them next, and then her smile, which looks unguarded enough that I immediately distrust my choice of adjective. People are not networks. A smile is not an open port. My therapist has never said this exact sentence, but only because I haven’t given her sufficient technical context. Maya stands when I reach the table. I almost offer a handshake. Excellent. Romance by enterprise onboarding. *** I used to break into systems without permission. Now companies pay me to discover why their systems deserve better companies. The difference is paperwork, authorization, and several years of learning that being capable of something does not constitute a reason to do it. Mostly I have learned. The reservation tablet probably shouldn’t display customer phone numbers. I turn my chair. Maya asks about my work. I give the version without war stories, because nothing says emotionally available like reminiscing about felony-adjacent adolescence. “Security testing,” I say. “Finding problems before somebody worse does.” She considers that. “So professionally suspicious.” Unfortunately, she makes it sound attractive. *** Her first breadcrumb arrives with the bread. She grew up in a town I’ve never heard of, outside a city everyone has. Her mother still lives on Juniper Lane. Their first dog was named Professor Pickles. A ridiculous name. A lovely name. A name that belongs in a story about a small girl giving a terrier elaborate academic credentials. Also exactly the kind of answer a badly designed recovery form might request. I hate that the second thought gets equal billing. She tells me the dog ate a library book. I ask which book. This feels like choosing the correct door in a burning building. *** The swords are from a fantasy series I haven’t read. I confess this, expecting the small conversational stall where mutual interests go to die. Instead she asks what kind of nerd I am. There are taxonomies. There are subspecies. There are people who own several mechanical keyboards and still believe they have made sensible financial decisions. “Magic,” I say. Her eyebrows rise. “The Gathering?” No, Maya, intimate birthday-party illusions. Please stop smiling or I will become unbearable. She plays Commander. I play Commander. For once, the thing unfolding in my head is not an incident report. *** She runs a graveyard deck and claims it isn’t annoying. This is demonstrably untrue, and I tell her so. She asks what I play. Mono-white. “Oh,” she says. “You’re the police.” I laugh hard enough that the waiter pauses beside us. A real laugh. Not the carefully timed acknowledgment I sometimes deploy when I’m occupied with the person behind someone, watching a bag unattended beneath a chair. Now I’m watching her hands describe an extremely stupid board state. She remembers every card. I remember every word. *** Dinner arrives without my noticing the waiter approach. That feels significant. We argue about whether a spectacular loss is better than an efficient win. She favors spectacle. I claim to favor efficiency, then admit I once spent forty minutes constructing a combo that accomplished nothing except making a goat enormous. She nearly drops her fork. This is going well. Not going-well-because-I-found-the-right-input. Actually well. She surprises me. I surprise myself. There is no script I can inspect, no response I can reproduce. I want another hour of this. Her phone lights up beside her plate. *** She unlocks it with a single, uncomplicated sweep. An L. Not subtly. Not shielded. A bright little diagram beneath her finger, visible from my chair. My brain supplies an assessment. My mouth, demonstrating catastrophic governance, publishes it. “That’s a really weak unlock pattern.” Her hand stops. The enormous goat dies alone. *** I could recover immediately. A normal person could recover immediately. Instead I add, “Someone watching could remember it.” There. Much better. Now she knows someone watching has remembered it. She places the phone facedown. “Were you watching?” The correct answer is yes, accidentally, followed by an apology. The answer my defensive little hindbrain prefers involves peripheral vision, professional conditioning, and how noticing differs from intending. All technically relevant. All profoundly beside the point. “I noticed,” I say. “I shouldn’t have commented like that. Sorry.” *** She studies me. I resist studying the study. This is harder than it sounds. “What else have you noticed?” The tablet. The cameras. The unattended bag. Her hometown, her childhood street, Professor Pickles with his terrible literary appetite. I could list everything. I could demonstrate how dangerous the world is and how useful I might be inside it. I recognize that impulse from client meetings: frighten them first, then sell reassurance. God. Absolutely not. “You’re funny,” I say. Then wince. That sounds evasive because it is. “I notice security stuff automatically. Sometimes I forget nobody asked for an audit.” *** She draws a line through the condensation on her glass. “I was having a nice time.” Was. A tiny word with teeth. “So was I.” “Then try being here.” No elaborate riddle. No hidden mechanism. Just a request I can meet or fail to meet. I put my phone away, although it has done nothing wrong. For a moment neither of us speaks. I let the silence remain unsolved. Then she asks whether my enormous goat had trample. It did not. Maya closes her eyes in theatrical grief. I laugh, cautiously this time, and tell her how I lost. When dessert comes, I notice her earrings catch the light. I had forgotten the swords.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical execution and creative understanding of the prompt. The author successfully captures the mindset of a reformed hacker through a distinctive internal voice that constantly oscillates between human connection and security assessment. The narrative structure using section breaks creates effective pacing and mirrors the protagonist's fragmented attention. The characterization is particularly well-crafted. The protagonist feels authentic - their automatic threat assessment ("three exits, two cameras") immediately establishes their mindset, while their self-awareness ("This is not a charming fact about me") adds depth and humor. The voice remains consistent throughout, balancing technical knowledge with genuine vulnerability. The Magic: The Gathering shared interest serves as an effective bridge between the characters, providing believable common ground that allows genuine connection to develop. The dialogue feels natural and reveals character - Maya's "You're the police" comment about mono-white decks shows personality while advancing the relationship dynamic. The central conflict around the phone unlock pattern is well-executed. The protagonist's inability to suppress their observation feels true to character, and their immediate recognition of the social misstep creates genuine tension. The recovery attempt and Maya's response ("Then try being here") provides a realistic resolution that doesn't feel artificially positive. The prose style is clean and purposeful, with effective use of short, punchy sentences that mirror the protagonist's analytical thinking. Metaphors like "A tiny word with teeth" and "Romance by enterprise onboarding" feel fresh and character-appropriate. However, some elements could be stronger. The ending, while sweet, feels slightly rushed in its resolution. The transition from tension back to comfort happens quickly, though it's not entirely unearned given the established connection. Some of the technical security observations, while character-appropriate, occasionally feel inserted primarily to demonstrate expertise rather than serving the narrative. The piece succeeds in creating emotional complexity - the protagonist's struggle between their nature and their desire for connection feels genuine and relatable. The humor throughout prevents the piece from becoming too heavy while maintaining emotional stakes. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 88.4
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Overthinking It The projector squeaks whenever Ms. Alvarez changes slides, like a mouse being mildly inconvenienced. I have counted eleven squeaks since she said we could choose partners. Eleven opportunities to turn toward Eli and say something normal. Except now he has chosen me, which should simplify things. It has not simplified things. “Want to work together?” he asked. I said, “Sure.” A reasonable response. Practically elegant. Unfortunately, I also nodded four times, so the overall effect was probably less *casual lab partner* and more *dashboard ornament on a gravel road*. Now he is moving his chair beside mine. Beside. Mine. There should be a procedure for this. We have procedures for chemical spills and broken glass, but apparently if a boy with excellent eyebrows voluntarily enters your personal space, you’re just supposed to know where your elbows go. Mine are on the table. Is that aggressive? Taking up territory? I put them in my lap. Now I look like I’m waiting for disappointing medical news. Squeak. Our assignment appears: design an experiment testing how temperature affects the rate at which sugar dissolves. Good. Science. I understand science. Variables don’t secretly think you’re annoying. A thermometer never tells another thermometer what you said at lunch. I could say, *We should keep the amount of sugar constant.* That would establish competence without suggesting I have imagined what it would be like if he waited for me outside English. Which I have not done excessively. Only on days when we have English. We have English daily. “We should probably—” “So, hot water?” he says. We both stop. Wonderful. A collision. There should be little airbags in conversations. “Sorry,” I say. “No, go ahead.” Now I have the floor, which is worse than not having it. The floor is enormous. People can fall through floors. *We should keep the amount of sugar constant.* The sentence is right there, polished and waiting. Inside my head, I could explain controlled variables to a congressional committee. Outside my head, my tongue has become a damp mitten. “Same sugar,” I say. Eli looks at the worksheet. “Yeah. Like, one teaspoon each?” “Yes.” Excellent. I have contributed two words and a confirmation. At this rate, I’ll complete a sentence by graduation. He writes *one teaspoon* in the planning box. His handwriting slopes upward, as if every word is hopeful about something. Do not stare at his handwriting. That is a weird thing to stare at. Look at the worksheet. Not his hand holding the worksheet. The actual worksheet, you absolute disaster. Squeak. I should ask him a question. People like questions. Except questions can sound like interviews, and interviews can sound like you’ve prepared, and preparing can sound desperate. *Did you understand the homework?* No. He’ll think I’m offering tutoring. Or requesting tutoring. Either version introduces an unnecessary power imbalance. *Are you going to the basketball game Friday?* Dangerous. If he says yes, I have to produce another sentence. If he says no, I also have to produce another sentence. There is no safe branch on that decision tree. *Nice pencil.* Please evacuate the decision tree. He taps his eraser against the table. “Do we stir them?” I know this one. “If we do, we’d have to stir each cup at the same speed, or stirring becomes another variable.” The whole sentence comes out. Intact. For a second, I’m so relieved I almost smile directly at him. Then I worry that smiling after mentioning variables suggests an unhealthy attachment to experimental design. But he nods. “Right. So no stirring.” Right. He said *right*. Not *wow, you’re unbearable*. Interesting. Evidence worth collecting. Across the room, Maya laughs, and my shoulders tighten before I can stop them. She is not laughing at me. She’s facing the sink. Someone probably did something near the sink. Unless she looked over first. Unless I said *variable* strangely. I replay it. VAIR-ee-uh-bull. Normal pronunciation, probably. My voice might have gone higher at the end. I wish my brain would stop assigning itself detective work when there isn’t even a crime. Eli slides the worksheet between us. “You want to draw the setup? You’re good at drawing.” He knows that? Maybe he remembers my cell diagram from October. Maybe he notices everyone’s diagrams. Maybe this is simply an efficient allocation of labor and not a meaningful development requiring immediate analysis. “Okay,” I say, accepting the pencil he offers even though mine is literally in my hand. Now I have two pencils. A girl with options. I put mine down carefully. Too carefully. Nobody casually arranges a pencil parallel to a worksheet unless they are defusing it. Three cups. Three thermometers. Labels underneath. Drawing gives my hands an assignment other than revealing everything about me. I could ask him to label the temperatures. I could make that sound friendly. Or bossy. Probably bossy if I don’t smile, strange if I smile too much. My face is exhausting. Squeak. Eli glances toward the projector. “Is that thing okay?” There it is. An opening I didn’t have to manufacture. *It sounds like a mouse being mildly inconvenienced.* Funny in my head. Potentially baffling in the atmosphere. He might not laugh. He might do the polite nose-exhale adults do when you show them something they don’t understand. Or I could say nothing, and spend tonight constructing seventeen better versions of this exact moment while brushing my teeth. “It sounds,” I say, watching the cup I’m drawing, “like an annoyed mouse.” Eli laughs. Not loudly. Enough. “Every slide is ruining its day.” I look up before remembering to manage my expression. “Honestly, same.” He grins, and I grin back. Then I worry I grinned too long. Of course I do. The worry doesn’t disappear. It sits beside the relief while I label our cups, both of them taking up space. Still, when he asks what temperature we should try first, I answer without rehearsing. “Room temperature. We can start there.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional skill in capturing the authentic voice of an anxious 8th-grade girl through internal monologue. The writer successfully creates a believable character whose intelligence shines through her overthinking, while her social anxiety creates realistic barriers to expression. The narrative structure is tight and focused, maintaining engagement throughout without meandering. The prose style is particularly strong, employing clever metaphors ("dashboard ornament on a gravel road," "damp mitten" for her tongue) that feel natural to the character's voice rather than forced literary flourishes. The writing captures the exhausting mental gymnastics of social anxiety with remarkable authenticity - the constant second-guessing, the analysis of micro-expressions, and the gap between internal articulation and external fumbling. Character development is nuanced and consistent. The protagonist's intelligence comes through in her scientific knowledge and witty internal observations, while her anxiety manifests in believable physical behaviors (the four nods, pencil arrangement, shoulder tightening). The ending strikes an appropriate balance - she experiences a small victory without any unrealistic transformation of her fundamental anxiety. The dialogue, though minimal as requested, feels natural and age-appropriate. The interaction flows believably, with realistic interruptions and the awkward dance of teenage conversation. The piece effectively shows rather than tells the character's emotional state through specific details and behaviors. The writing maintains excellent pacing and coherence, with each paragraph building naturally on the previous one. The science project setting provides perfect structure for the internal drama. The voice remains consistent throughout - intelligent but anxious, self-aware but trapped in overthinking patterns. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the metaphors, while clever, might slightly exceed what feels natural for the character's age, though this is balanced by the overall authenticity of voice. Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
At four percent, my phone becomes a small animal I am responsible for keeping alive. I dim the screen until Sam’s last message is barely visible. *Running ten minutes late. Can’t wait to see you.* The second sentence is obviously there to soften the first. Or it is a second sentence. I put the phone facedown. The blue shirt says I think this is a date. The black shirt says I have recovered from thinking this is a date. We have been friends for six years and sleeping together for three weeks, which apparently means I no longer know how to wear clothes. *I think we moved too fast,* Sam will say. *You moved,* I’ll say. *You kissed me in your kitchen.* No. That sounds prosecutorial. I should be generous, devastatingly calm. *I understand. I just wish you’d been honest.* That is better. That gives me the moral advantage without revealing that I spent Tuesday checking whether they had watched my story. They have been distant. This is a fact, except when I examine it. Two shorter messages. One canceled lunch because their father needed a ride from the hospital. Falling asleep during our usual evening conversation. People with fathers in hospitals still have thumbs. What an ugly thought. But people can use real difficulties as cover. Both things can be true. I am very good at finding a version where both things are true and one of them means nobody loves me. Three percent. I find the charger beneath the bed, wrapped around a slipper. It only works at an angle. So do I, apparently. *You need too much reassurance.* *I need basic communication.* *I can’t be responsible for your feelings.* *I never asked you to be.* Except I have asked, indirectly, repeatedly, in messages dressed as jokes. *Still like me or should I move countries?* A little clown holding a genuine emergency. Sam always answers. That should count. It counts until the next time. I know what my therapist would call this. I know the phrase “abandonment alarm,” and I know my borderline diagnosis is not a prophecy. But knowing the name of an alarm does not make the building feel less on fire. I put on the black shirt. Then the blue. The phone vibrates against the floor. *Got us the corner table. Your favorite terrible painting is still here.* They remembered. Something in my chest opens so abruptly it hurts. The painting: a pear that looks like it owes someone money. Our joke. Six years of shared evidence. They got there early enough to choose the table, even running late. Unless they chose familiar surroundings to make this easier. I unplug the phone at five percent. On the walk, I prepare not to cry. Crying will make them stay out of guilt, and staying out of guilt is worse than leaving, although leaving is also worse than everything. *We can still be friends.* *Actually, I don’t think we can.* I enjoy that answer. I enjoy, for half a block, the imagined shock on their face. Let them lose something. Let them discover that access to me is not permanent. Then I picture never hearing their laugh again and nearly walk into a parking meter. They stand when I reach the table. Not halfway. Fully, smiling, arms already opening. “You look lovely.” I step into the hug with my body held carefully away, then give up and press close. Their hand settles between my shoulders. Familiar pressure. I could live inside this pressure. I could hate them for knowing how to do it. “You too,” I say. They kiss me, briefly, on the mouth. Here. In public. I had prepared for a careful cheek. For several seconds there is no argument available. There is just their cold nose against mine and the smell of rain in their coat. Then: perhaps affection is easy for them. Perhaps I am mistaking ease for meaning. They have ordered the olives I like. I decide this is tenderness, then preparation. Their knees touch mine beneath the table. I decide this is accidental, until they leave them there. “I’ve missed you,” they say. *Then where have you been?* The answer arrives with a photograph: their father at home, grinning beneath a blanket, giving the camera an irritated thumbs-up. “Sorry I’ve been patchy. It’s been a week.” They look tired. There are shadows under their eyes I somehow omitted from every rehearsal. I want to be someone who notices tiredness before danger. Instead I say, “I thought maybe things were weird.” Their face softens, which is wonderful and unbearable. Now they know. Now I am the person who needs this conversation. “Not weird. New, maybe. Good new.” My relief is so large it embarrasses me. I look down, pretending to rearrange my napkin. *Good new.* I want it in writing. I want tomorrow included. My phone lights up: one percent. “Oh,” Sam says. “Here.” They take a battery pack from their bag, plug in a cable, slide it across. They remembered my broken charger. I told them days ago. This is care. I let the thought stand without an objection for one whole breath. Then I wonder whether they keep it for everyone. Of course they do. It is a battery pack. Sam asks about my interview. They remember the interviewer’s name. I start answering, then hear myself making the story entertaining, easy to love. But they laugh before the punchline, at something I hadn’t polished. For a moment I stop performing. Under the table, I uncurl one hand. Sam takes it. I let them, while checking their face for the first sign that they want it back.

+ Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 86.3
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Blood Debt The temple’s gods had lost their faces before the duelists were born. Beneath them, men counted silver. One torch burned in an iron bracket on the western pillar. Its light reached the rectangular fighting floor, the broken altar at its northern end, and the doorway opposite. Beyond that rectangle, spectators crowded the walls. They had agreed to keep the floor clear. Nobody had agreed to intervene. Arata entered from the north carrying an oak practice sword. Liang waited near the southern doorway with empty hands. Their masters had forbidden this meeting separately, furiously, and for almost identical reasons. Three generations of insults had already purchased six funerals. Neither school needed another boy mistaken for an argument. Arata had come anyway. So had Liang. “The sword stays?” Liang asked. “You challenged my school.” “I challenged you.” Arata lowered the wooden point toward Liang’s throat. “There is no difference.” Behind him, his supporters murmured approval. Liang heard someone call him a porter’s son. He was a porter’s son. His father’s shoulders had bought every lesson he had ever taken. He rolled those same broad shoulders once. They stood three long paces apart, Arata facing south, Liang north. Dust covered the flagstones, but the central strip remained sound. Along the eastern edge, a fallen roof beam lay parallel to the wall. Liang noticed it. Arata watched Liang. Then Arata lifted his sword beside his right shoulder, its tip slanting upward behind him. The room quieted. His first attack consumed the distance. A stamping advance, a tearing shout, and the oak blade descended toward Liang’s crown. Nothing tentative preceded it. Arata had spent years striking upright timber until his hands blistered and his whole body learned to arrive behind one blow. Liang slipped east, to his own right. The sword passed his left shoulder. Before Arata could recover it, Liang swung his left forearm across the exposed left side of Arata’s head. Arata folded his elbows and turned toward him. The sword’s rising hilt intercepted Liang’s forearm. Bone struck oak. Liang withdrew with his fingers tingling. They now faced each other across the eastern half of the floor: Arata nearer the center, Liang nearer the fallen beam. “Fast enough to run,” Arata said. Liang smiled without pleasure. “Slow enough to talk.” He advanced behind a loose right-hand sweep toward Arata’s eyes. Arata thrust the sword straight at his chest. Liang twisted clockwise, drawing his right shoulder back. The point grazed his jacket instead of entering his sternum. His left palm slapped the shaft sideways, but Arata immediately retracted it, denying him a grip. Liang’s turning momentum carried his right arm around in a low, whipping arc. His palm struck Arata above the left hip. It landed cleanly. It did not stop him. Arata stepped into the contact and drove the sword’s hilt toward Liang’s face. Liang jerked backward. The pommel split his lower lip. A cheer struck the ceiling. He retreated east one step. His heel touched the fallen beam. Arata saw the interruption and raised the sword. Liang could not retreat again. He sprang south instead, along the beam, as the downward blow cracked against the timber where his ankle had been. Splinters scattered across his trousers. Arata wrenched the sword free and pivoted south. Liang was already moving north again. The reversal brought him inside the lifting weapon. He planted his left foot beside Arata’s right and snapped his right forearm upward beneath the sword hand. Arata’s wrists rose. His next cut stalled overhead. Liang’s left hand whipped toward his jaw. Arata tucked his chin. The palm struck cheek rather than throat, turning his face but leaving his balance intact. He answered with his forehead. Their skulls collided. Liang staggered south. Arata stumbled north, blinking. For a moment, neither attacked. Blood darkened Liang’s teeth. A swelling ridge lifted above Arata’s eyebrow. Between them, the torch made their shadows strike and retreat without their permission. “Finish him,” somebody whispered. Arata heard his grandfather’s name behind him, invoked like a debt collector. Liang heard laughter from the northern wall. Both came forward. Arata cut diagonally from his right shoulder toward Liang’s left hip. Liang checked his advance. The sword swept past his stomach, close enough to drag the loose cloth of his jacket. As it passed, he stepped northwest, outside Arata’s right arm. His right palm struck the back of Arata’s sword hand. His left forearm followed across the right elbow. The blows forced the extended weapon lower. Liang crowded closer, chest almost against Arata’s shoulder, denying him room to swing. He hooked his right foot behind Arata’s forward ankle and drove diagonally across his back. Arata fell onto his left knee. He kept the sword. Liang reached over his right shoulder, caught the grip below his hands, and pulled upward. Arata resisted, elbows tight. Then Liang stamped down on the blade. Oak broke against stone. Silence replaced the betting. Arata stared at the shortened weapon. Liang stood behind his right shoulder, breathing through his open mouth. One hard blow to the temple remained available. He raised his hand. Arata saw the shadow rise on the floor. Neither moved. From the darkness came the scrape of someone drawing steel. Liang lowered his hand. “No,” he said. Whether he spoke to the spectator, to Arata, or to himself, nobody could tell. He stepped backward toward the southern doorway, leaving Arata room to stand. Arata rose slowly. The broken sword trembled in his grip. “You think sparing me makes you better?” Liang pressed his tongue against his torn lip. “No. I think killing you makes your brother come looking for mine.” The torch guttered. Men shifted along the walls, suddenly conscious of how narrow the doorway was. Arata looked toward his supporters. None offered to meet his eyes. At last, he placed the broken sword on the floor. Liang left first. No money changed hands until both were gone. Then the witnesses began arguing over who had won, carefully preserving the thing the fighters had almost ended.

[Analysis] This piece demonstrates strong technical craft and adherence to the prompt's demanding requirements. The author successfully creates a vivid underground duel between representatives of the specified martial arts styles, maintaining excellent spatial awareness throughout the fight choreography. The setting of the ruined temple is economically but effectively established, and the social dynamics between the schools are woven naturally into the narrative. The fight choreography is particularly impressive, with precise tracking of both fighters' positions, movements, and the physics of their combat. Each strike, counter, and spatial shift is clearly visualized without becoming mechanical or overly technical. The author demonstrates deep understanding of both fighting styles, showing Arata's explosive, decisive Jigen-ryū attacks against Liang's evasive, circular Piguaquan techniques. The prose style is lean and controlled, with strong economy of language. Sentences like "The temple's gods had lost their faces before the duelists were born" establish both setting and historical weight efficiently. The dialogue is sparse but effective, revealing character through brief exchanges that feel natural to the tense situation. Character development is subtle but present. Both fighters are given clear motivations rooted in class conflict and family honor, and their actions remain consistent with their backgrounds. Liang's final decision to spare Arata feels earned through the established stakes and his practical wisdom about escalating cycles of violence. The ending avoids both false positivity and overwrought darkness. The ambiguous resolution - where neither fighter truly wins and the underlying tensions remain - feels authentic to the situation. The final image of witnesses arguing over who won while "carefully preserving the thing the fighters had almost ended" is particularly sophisticated. Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
# Breaking Formation The clock above the mirror reads 00:18:00 when Master Han tells us we have not started working yet. My shirt is already soaked. Sweat runs beneath the elastic waistband of the academy’s practice trousers, which cost more than the shoes I won my scholarship in. Those shoes wait against the rear wall, soles separating, beside eleven pairs that look delivered this morning. Here, even exhaustion seems to require the right equipment. I stand on the center mark of the back row, four meters from the mirror. Three trainees occupy the front row, two meters ahead. In my row, Minseo stands a meter and a half to my left; Jun stands the same distance to my right. Six bodies, two straight rows. White tape crosses beneath each pair of feet. “Again. No traveling beyond the marks.” Han stands beside the mirror’s left edge. I knew his face before I knew Seoul: rehearsal videos, survival shows, contestants thanking him through tears. Online, they called him the man who broke bad habits. At orientation, someone whispered that habits were only where he started. The combination traces a small square and returns us home. On one, my right foot steps half a meter right; both forearms punch forward at shoulder height. Two: left foot closes beside right, elbows retract. Three: left foot steps half a meter toward the mirror, arms dropping straight beside my thighs. Four: right foot closes, sternum hits forward once. Five: right foot steps backward into its previous place, right arm slicing diagonally down across my chest. Six: left foot closes beside it. Seven: left foot steps half a meter left, elbows clamping against my ribs. Eight: right foot closes; chin snaps level. No bounce. No preparation visible. The joints must announce each number separately. At home, behind the boarded laundromat, we danced around the pothole nobody could afford to fill. Somebody’s speaker clipped every bass note. You learned to let a broken sound travel through you: ankle, knee, pelvis, shoulder. A groove made the spaces between beats inhabitable. Here, the spaces are property I am trespassing on. 00:15:42. “One, two, three, four—” My sternum strikes on four, but muscle memory keeps talking. The hit becomes a body roll, ribs softening down toward my stomach. My knees bend to receive it. By five, when everybody else’s right foot has landed backward, mine is only lifting. I rush the backward step, close on six, move left on seven. On eight, I reach my original cross with my weight still rocking toward my heels. In the mirror, five chins stop. Mine floats. Han cuts the music. “Your chest.” I flatten a palm against it. “Not injured,” he says. “Undisciplined.” A couple of trainees look down. I cannot tell whether that is embarrassment for me or protection from him. My Korean is good enough for corrections and not good enough for whatever follows them under someone’s breath. “Popping uses a release,” I say. “So does this. You are adding one.” He demonstrates from beside the mirror: sternum forward, sternum neutral. No rolling descent. A clean contraction, then nothing. He is right. That makes the heat in my face worse. 00:12:06. We repeat. My thighs begin trembling during the holds. Han makes us freeze on four, feet together half a meter right and half a meter forward of our starting crosses. The front row is now a meter and a half from the mirror; mine is three and a half meters away. Our forearms hang still. Six lifted breastbones. Six mouths trying not to gasp. He walks along the studio’s left wall, passes the front row, then turns behind us. I track him through the mirror until Jun’s shoulder hides him. “You,” he says behind me. “Stay. Others, finish.” The other five step backward on five, close on six, left on seven, close on eight. I remain forward and right of my mark. They are statues around an empty place where I belong. Han comes around my right side and stops an arm’s length away, outside my little square. “Finish.” I step backward with my right foot. Close left. Step left. Close right. Now my cross is beneath me again. “You can find it slowly,” he says. “Stop pretending you cannot find it fast.” “I’m not pretending.” “You make every correction an argument.” The clock reads 00:08:19. My scholarship covers tuition, a dormitory bed, meals that arrive in portions I still misjudge. It does not cover going home defeated. My mother has shown the acceptance email to people who cannot read it. She cleaned offices overnight while I practiced on concrete. I hear her asking whether I am eating. I hear my old crew asking why my shoulders look locked. Han steps backward toward the right wall, clearing our row. “Alone. Eight counts.” The music starts. One: right. Two: close. Three: forward. Four arrives, and there is the door in my chest: hit, melt, let the movement spill downward. I could open it. Make him watch something he cannot count. Instead I hit and release to neutral. Five: backward. Six: close. Seven: left. Eight: together. My feet cover the tape. The silence afterward feels less like victory than holding my breath underwater. Han nods once. “There. Now choose it again.” 00:05:03. He brings the others back into motion. This time I watch Minseo’s reflection without turning my head. Her stops are exact, but she is not empty inside them. On two, her elbows retract with a sharpness mine lack; on four, her sternum hits without dragging her belly after it. She has learned where effort belongs. I try again. The square stays square. My chest stops when I tell it to. I cannot yet tell whether I am gaining a tool or building a cage. For now, I refuse to confuse unfamiliar with false. The clock reaches 00:00:00 as my right foot closes on eight. Under my ribs, the next movement waits. I leave it there, mine to begin.

Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bailiff struck the floor with a bone belonging to no recognized animal. “All rise.” Everyone rose except the witness chair, which had been found in contempt that morning. Dream regarded the assembled court. His expression did not change, but several candles shortened themselves. “First Love against Mora,” said the clerk. “Trespass, unlawful alteration of emotional weather, and consumption of resources without the dreamer’s consent.” “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” said Mora. “We have not reached your defense.” “Just establishing it.” Her faint cackle rose into the vaults. It returned from somewhere overhead sounding slightly nearer. First Love stood at the plaintiff’s table, rosy-cheeked, holding a folder tied with ribbon. He had brought flowers. Under the circumstances, they looked like evidence. “My lord, I spent eleven weeks cultivating this dream.” “Describe it.” “A meadow. Late afternoon. Wildflowers, but nothing aggressively symbolic. Max lies beside the girl he likes. They talk. Neither remembers the conversation afterward, only that it went well.” “Max being?” “Eighteen. Final year of school. Inclined to rehearse greetings and then say something entirely different.” Dream inclined his head. A familiar jurisdiction. “And the conclusion?” “An almost-kiss. Deliberately muddled. He wakes happy, embarrassed, and unable to decide what it means.” “You consider this satisfactory?” “Formative,” said First Love. Mora made a small noise through her nose. The clerk wrote *defendant scoffs*. “I breathed,” Mora said. “We shall endeavor to distinguish the two.” *** The meadow appeared above the evidence table. Max lay among the flowers beside a girl in a blue cardigan. She was laughing. He looked as though he had personally invented laughter and was relieved it worked. “The lighting alone took three nights,” First Love said. The girl leaned over Max, playfully pinning his shoulders. “Here,” said First Love, gripping his folder. Her shadow moved against the sun. The flowers folded shut. The girl’s smile stayed almost unchanged, which was worse than if it had widened. Her eyes darkened; her hair fell forward in strands that did not obey gravity. She settled upon Max’s chest. He tried to move. He could not. A pale thread slipped between his lips. Mora leaned toward the exhibit with professional interest. “Pause there.” The clerk froze the scene. “What?” asked Dream. “Nothing. Good consistency.” First Love stared at her. “That is his breath.” “Yes.” “You say that as though I’ve mislabeled a jam.” “Have you ever tried living on symbolism?” Dream lifted one finger. The exhibit vanished. For a moment the court heard Max struggling to wake. Then that, too, ceased. The candles grew shorter. *** “Your defense,” said Dream. Mora rose. She wore black, although certain portions of it appeared to be holes. “The meadow was unguarded.” “It is a dream,” said First Love. “Not a warehouse.” “All the more reason to post someone.” “You entered under the likeness of his crush.” “Established access point.” “You corrupted a tender experience.” “I diversified it.” Her cackle traveled upward. Something in the ceiling shifted away. Dream looked at her. Mora folded her hands. “My lord, I am a nightmare spirit. I sit on chests. I cause paralysis and terror. There are limits to how creatively I can interpret the position.” “And the breath?” “Meals are not generally provided.” First Love untied his folder with trembling fingers. “I submit that the defendant’s alterations have contaminated the entire emotional structure. He remains fond of the girl. He also fears that she may open her mouth and release beetles.” “Only once,” Mora said. “He now becomes anxious whenever she leans across a desk.” “He was anxious before.” “For different reasons.” “Can you prove that?” First Love opened his mouth, then closed it. The clerk looked almost cheerful. *** Dream rested one hand upon the arm of his throne. It was not a large movement. Both advocates stopped breathing, though only one had a legitimate use for the habit. “Who owns this meadow?” he asked. “I made it,” said First Love. “I occupied it,” said Mora. “That was not my question.” Silence settled. From the witness chair came a faint wooden creak. “The boy,” said Dream. First Love lowered his eyes. Mora considered this. “Does he have representation?” “He is asleep.” “Convenient.” The courtroom doors shut themselves. “Withdrawn,” she said. Dream examined the meadow now reflected in the black surface of his ring. There were simpler judgments available. He could expel Mora. He could restore the flowers, adjust the afternoon, return the almost-kiss to its appointed uncertainty. He had spent the preceding century settling a dispute between two prophetic wells. “Clerk,” he said. “A joint tenancy.” First Love went pale. Mora brightened. “Subject to conditions.” Mora stopped brightening. *** That night Max dreamed of a courtroom. He stood accused of Having Feelings. The charge sheet was fourteen pages long. Most of the evidence consisted of things he had said in corridors. Mora presided from behind a desk, wearing a headmistress’s gown and an expression of restrained hunger. “This is degrading,” she had told Dream. “You may appeal.” “To whom?” Dream had looked at her. Now she tapped her papers. “Did you, on Tuesday, say ‘you too’ when the young lady wished you luck with your examination?” Max discovered that the public gallery contained everyone he had ever met. “Yes,” he whispered. Mora inhaled the frightened breath he willingly let out. Under the order, she could take nothing held within him. A door opened. The girl in the blue cardigan entered. “I’ll speak for him,” she said. First Love, concealed beneath counsel’s table, shut his eyes with relief. She took Max’s hand. The gallery disappeared. Almost. Mora remained, chewing discreetly. *** Dream received the report before dawn. “Successful?” he asked. “The boy woke pleasantly confused,” said the clerk. “Mora lodged an objection.” “On what grounds?” “The almost-kiss occurred during her summation.” Dream’s mouth moved slightly. “Overruled.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece demonstrates exceptional craft in executing a complex prompt that demanded a delicate balance of dark fantasy, comedy, and courtroom drama. The author successfully creates a vivid Court of the Dreaming that feels both otherworldly and bureaucratically familiar, achieving the requested intersection of fantastical and mundane elements. The characterization is particularly strong. Dream's irritation manifests through subtle environmental cues (candles shortening, doors shutting themselves) rather than explicit emotional displays, maintaining his canonical inscrutability while conveying his mood. Mora's pragmatic defense ("a girl's gotta eat too") and professional pride in her nightmare craft create a compelling antagonist who isn't purely villainous. First Love's earnest dedication to his romantic craft provides effective contrast. The dialogue crackles with wit and authenticity. Each character has a distinct voice - Dream's formal, measured speech; Mora's casual pragmatism; First Love's artistic sensibility. The courtroom procedural elements are handled with dry humor that never undermines the fantasy setting. The prose style is admirably restrained, following the instruction to use descriptives sparingly. Lines like "Everyone rose except the witness chair, which had been found in contempt that morning" exemplify the understated dark humor requested. The writing avoids purple prose while maintaining atmospheric richness through selective, precise details. The resolution demonstrates genuine creativity. Rather than a simple victory for either party, Dream's joint tenancy solution creates new complications that serve the story's themes. The final courtroom dream sequence cleverly inverts the power dynamic while maintaining the established rules of the world. The pacing is excellent, moving efficiently through exposition, conflict, and resolution without feeling rushed. The sectional breaks provide natural breathing room and help structure the narrative flow. Minor weaknesses include occasional moments where the humor could be sharper, and some transitions between sections feel slightly abrupt. However, these are minimal concerns in an otherwise polished piece that successfully fulfills a challenging creative brief.
